0.title: 2 Corinthians: Strength in Weakness
0.overview:
Second Corinthians is the most autobiographical of Paul's letters and, by many measures, the most emotionally raw document in the New Testament. Where Romans is a theological treatise and Galatians a polemical defence of the gospel, 2 Corinthians is a window into the interior life of an apostle under siege — attacked by opponents, misunderstood by the very church he founded, exhausted by suffering, and yet mysteriously sustained by a grace he cannot fully explain. It is the letter in which Paul most fully exposes the paradox at the heart of the Christian life: strength made perfect in weakness, treasure carried in jars of clay, life produced through death.

The letter was written from Macedonia, probably in AD 55–56, after a painful sequence of events: a “painful visit” to Corinth that went badly (2:1), a severe letter that followed (2:3–4; 7:8), anxiety about how the Corinthians would respond, and then the relief of Titus's report that most had repented (7:6–7). Paul writes in the aftermath of that partial reconciliation, addressing a church that has largely come back to him — but not entirely, since a group of opponents (often called the “super-apostles” or “false apostles”) still commands a following and challenges his authority.

How many letters did Paul write to Corinth? At least four. An early letter, now lost, warned against associating with the sexually immoral (1 Cor 5:9); then came 1 Corinthians; then a painful visit (2:1); then a letter written with many tears (2:4; 7:8); and then this one. Many scholars think chapters 10–13 are part of that tearful letter, or a later one, because the tone changes so sharply at chapter 10. But no manuscript ever divides the letter; the tearful letter was written to grieve them over an offence, which chapters 10–13 never mention; and the change of tone is explained by Paul turning from the repentant majority (chapters 1–9) to the false apostles still at work. The more likely reading is that 2 Corinthians is one letter, and the tearful letter is lost.

The letter falls into three broad movements. Chapters 1–7 address the ministry of suffering and reconciliation: Paul defends the authenticity of his apostleship by pointing to suffering as its credential, not its disqualification, and unfolds a breathtaking theology of the new covenant ministry. Chapters 8–9 address the collection for the Jerusalem church — a sustained theology of generosity rooted in the self-giving of Christ. Chapters 10–13, which contain the “fool's speech,” are Paul's sharp and ironic defence of his apostleship against the super-apostles, climaxing in the account of his thorn in the flesh and the word that defines the entire letter: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.”

The letter's central theological contribution is its theology of weakness and glory. Paul's opponents measured apostleship by rhetorical skill, impressive presence, and spiritual fireworks. Paul measures it by the cross: authentic ministry looks like dying and rising, like carrying in the body the death of Jesus so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested. This is not merely Paul's personal psychological coping; it is a fundamental claim about how the kingdom of God advances — through the cruciform shape of those who carry it.

1.title: The God of All Comfort and the Yes of Christ
1.overview:
Some background makes this letter far clearer. Corinth was a rich, proud, commercial city on the isthmus between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese, refounded by Julius Caesar as a Roman colony in 44 BC and full of ambitious freedmen on the way up. Status, eloquence and success mattered enormously there. Paul founded the church around AD 50 (Acts 18) and later wrote 1 Corinthians. Things went badly afterwards: he made a short “painful visit” in which someone in the church publicly opposed him (2:1–5), then wrote a severe letter “with many tears” (2:4), and changed his plan to visit again. Meanwhile visiting preachers, impressive speakers with letters of recommendation, were telling the church that Paul was weak, unreliable and second-rate. 2 Corinthians is Paul’s reply, written from Macedonia once Titus brought news that most of the church had repented (7:5–7).

Chapter 1 sets the theme of the whole letter: God’s power shows up in weakness. Paul begins by blessing the God of all comfort, who comforted him in an affliction so crushing he despaired of life, so that he can comfort others and learn to rely on God who raises the dead. Then he answers the charge that his changed travel plans prove he is fickle. His message is not “Yes and No”, because in Christ every promise of God is “Yes”; God has anointed and sealed his people with the Spirit as a down payment. He stayed away to spare them, not because he wants to lord it over their faith.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The God of All Comfort
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul opens by naming himself an apostle by God’s will, the very point his critics dispute. Then, instead of complaining about a terrible year, he praises God as the Father who shows compassion and gives strength in every kind of trouble. The comfort he receives is not for himself alone: it equips him to strengthen others in their troubles. His sufferings and the Corinthians’ are bound together, and so is the comfort. He tells them frankly that in Asia he was crushed beyond endurance and expected to die, and he sees the purpose: to stop relying on himself and rely on the God who raises the dead. That God rescued him and will do so again, helped by their prayers, so that many will give thanks.
verseByVerse.theology:
The phrase “Father of mercies and God of all comfort” (v. 3) is a carefully constructed title. “Mercies” is plural, and it echoes the Hebrew word for the deep, gut-level compassion that is related to the word for womb. “Comfort” shares its root with the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit, the Helper (John 14:16). God himself, through the Spirit he sends, is the source and supply of all genuine comfort. No human comfort is ultimate; all genuine comfort is God’s own comfort mediated through creaturely means.

The suffering-comfort dynamic in vv. 4–7 is the pastoral theology of the cross applied to ministry. The wound is the credential. Those who have been comforted in their own affliction have something to give that those who have only known ease cannot supply. This is not a glorification of suffering for its own sake but a recognition that God wastes nothing — not even the darkest experiences of his servants.
verseByVerse.examples:
A pastor who has gone through a severe depressive episode returns to ministry and finds that his counselling of those suffering from depression has taken on a different quality. He is not simply applying techniques; he is giving what he has received. His people sense it. This is the dynamic Paul describes — not therapeutic expertise but the transferable comfort of one who has been there and been comforted by the God who is there.

And v. 11 puts the same dynamic in reverse. A member of the congregation who has never taught, never led and never travelled prays through the week for a missionary she has met once. Paul’s sentence says that her praying is not a gesture of support alongside the real work; it is a shoulder genuinely under the load. Churches that publish requests and never report the outcomes rob such people of the best half of it — the thanksgiving that Paul says was the point of the rescue in the first place.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God that is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus because God willed it, and from our brother Timothy, to the church of God in Corinth, and to all God’s people throughout the province of Achaia: grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

By the will of God. In most letters this is a standard opening. Here it is the thesis. Visiting teachers in Corinth were saying Paul was no real apostle: unimpressive in person, a poor speaker, always in trouble, with no letters of recommendation (3:1; 10:10). Paul’s answer begins in the first line. He did not appoint himself, and the church did not appoint him. God did, on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:15).

The church of God that is at Corinth. After all the trouble, still “the church of God”. A church does not stop belonging to God because it is behaving badly.

Achaia. The Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital. There were believers in Cenchreae, Corinth’s eastern port (Romans 16:1), Athens (Acts 17:34) and elsewhere. The letter was meant to circulate.

On a Tuesday. If your authority to do what you do (as a parent, pastor, manager or elder) comes from God, you do not need to win every argument to keep it. You need to be faithful.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote this letter from Macedonia, probably around AD 55–56, after a painful visit to Corinth and a severe letter written “with many tears.” Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praise be to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of every kind of comfort.

Blessing first. Paul has just come through the worst year of his life (vv. 8–9). The first thing he writes is not complaint but praise. He took the Jewish prayer form “Blessed be God” (berakah) and filled it with Christ.

Father of mercies. A Hebrew way of saying “the merciful Father”, the one from whom all compassion comes. The plural “mercies” (oiktirmoi) echoes the Hebrew raḥamim, related to the word for womb: a mother’s tender compassion for her child. “As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you” (Isaiah 66:13). Compare “his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22–23).

God of all comfort. Paraklēsis: comfort, encouragement, strengthening; literally “calling alongside”. Its noun for a person, paraklētos, is Jesus’ name for the Holy Spirit, “another Helper” (John 14:16). Comfort here is not soothing or cheering up. It is God coming alongside to strengthen. The Old English “comfort” comes from Latin con-fortis, “with strength”, which is close. The word appears ten times in verses 3–7.

Isaiah’s comfort. “Comfort, comfort my people, says your God” (Isaiah 40:1) announced the end of exile and the coming of God himself. In Christ that comfort has arrived.

For worship. Bless God this week by these two names, in this order: Father of mercies, God of all comfort. Whatever is wrong, these are still true.

parallels.desc: I, I am he who comforts you

verseByVerse.quote: who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He comforts us in every trouble, so that we can comfort people in any trouble with the same comfort we ourselves receive from God.

So that. The key phrase. God’s comfort is not only for you; it is transferable. It becomes equipment for ministry.

All and any. God comforts us in “all” affliction, so we can comfort those in “any” affliction. Not just the same trouble we had. Someone who has been comforted by God in bereavement can help a person whose business has failed, because they have learned what God’s comfort is like.

Affliction. Thlipsis: pressure, crushing, like grapes in a press. The word will come again and again in this letter.

What it does not mean. Not that God sends suffering so that we can be useful, as if that were its only reason, or that you need to have gone through something to be any help at all. And not that comfort means saying the right words. Job’s friends were good comforters for seven days, while they sat in silence (Job 2:13); they went wrong when they started explaining.

On a Tuesday. A woman who lost a baby years ago, and was held by God through it, sits with a younger mother at the hospital. She does not offer explanations. She says, “I know. God carried me. He will carry you.” That is this verse.

parallels.desc: as one whom his mother comforts

verseByVerse.quote: For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For just as Christ’s sufferings overflow into our lives, so also through Christ our comfort overflows.

Christ’s sufferings in us. In what sense do Christians share Christ’s sufferings? Not by adding to the atonement, which is finished (Hebrews 10:12; John 19:30). Jesus asked Saul, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). The Head feels what happens to his body. When Paul is flogged for Christ, Christ counts the blows as falling on him.

Do our sufferings add merit? Roman Catholic teaching has used texts like this and Colossians 1:24 (“filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions”) to support the idea that the sufferings of saints add to a treasury of merit that can be applied to others. Verdict: Paul never says our sufferings atone for anyone. What is “lacking” in Christ’s afflictions is not their saving value but their extension to the church as the gospel goes out. Christ’s work for us is complete; his people now share his road.

Overflow, both ways. The same verb (perisseuō) on both sides. The sufferings overflow; so does the comfort, at the same rate. Not a promise that the pain will be small, but that it will never outrun the supply. If the flood rises, so does the boat.

Through Christ. The comfort comes through the one who was in it: misrepresented, abandoned by friends, crying out that God had forsaken him.

On a Tuesday. If you are mocked at work for your faith, or lose a friendship over it, remember that Christ takes it personally.

verseByVerse.quote: If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we are suffering, it is for your comfort and salvation. If we are comforted, that too is for your comfort, which works in you as you patiently endure the same sufferings we suffer.

For you. A startling claim. The Corinthians were comparing Paul unfavourably with impressive teachers while he was being crushed in Asia. He says the crushing was for them. Two ways: what he receives in trouble he passes on; and a church learns what the gospel can bear by seeing what it carries a man through.

And salvation. Not that Paul’s suffering saves them, but that it is one of the means God uses to keep them in the faith.

Patient endurance. Hypomonē: literally “remaining under”. Not gritted teeth and not resignation, but staying put under a weight instead of crawling out from under it. The comfort is found there, not by spectators.

A textual note. Manuscripts arrange the clauses of verses 6–7 in different orders, and the KJV follows a longer form. The sense is the same; the ESV follows the best early witnesses.

On a Tuesday. Your children, colleagues or church may be watching how you handle a hard diagnosis or a job loss. Your endurance may be the sermon they most need.

verseByVerse.quote: Our hope for you is unshaken, for we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our hope for you stands firm, because we know that just as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort.

Unshaken. Bebaia: firm, guaranteed, a legal word for a valid title deed. Paul’s hope for a troublesome church rests not on how they have behaved but on how God works.

Partners. Koinōnoi: sharers, partners, as in a business. Suffering and comfort are a joint account.

On a Tuesday. If you are a parent of a wayward child or a pastor of a difficult church, ground your hope where Paul does: not on their track record, but on God’s.

verseByVerse.quote: For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Friends, we want you to know about the trouble we went through in the province of Asia. We were crushed far beyond our strength, so much so that we despaired even of staying alive.

What happened? Paul does not say. Asia was the Roman province on the west coast of modern Turkey, with Ephesus as its capital. Suggestions:

The riot in Ephesus (Acts 19:23–41), though Acts does not say Paul himself was in mortal danger.

An imprisonment in Ephesus with a threatened death sentence, perhaps linked with “I fought with beasts at Ephesus” (1 Corinthians 15:32), which may be a metaphor for violent opponents.

A severe illness.

Verdict: we cannot know. The silence may be a mercy: whatever is crushing you fits the gap.

The words. “Utterly” is kath’ hyperbolēn, “beyond all measure” (our word hyperbole). “Beyond our strength” is past the limit of what he could carry. “Despaired” (exaporeomai) means to have no way out, every road blocked.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul lost his faith. He despaired of life, not of God. But it does mean that a real Christian, even an apostle in the middle of a fruitful ministry, can come to a place of utter darkness. Elijah asked to die (1 Kings 19:4). Jeremiah cursed the day he was born (Jeremiah 20:14). Jesus himself said, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Matthew 26:38). For a Christian struggling with depression or suicidal thoughts, who has been told that a real believer could never feel this way, this verse is oxygen.

On a Tuesday. If you or someone you love is in that place, say so to someone. Paul did, in a letter read aloud to a church that already thought him weak. Get help: a pastor, a doctor, a friend. And if the danger is immediate, phone emergency services or a crisis line today.
verseByVerse.note: Paul does not say what the danger in Asia was; it may have been the riot at Ephesus, severe illness or another threat.

verseByVerse.quote: Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In fact, inside ourselves we felt we had received the death sentence. But this happened so that we would stop trusting in ourselves and trust in God, who raises the dead.

The sentence of death. Apokrima: an official verdict, a court’s answer to a petition. Inside, Paul felt the case was closed.

That was to make us. Looking back, Paul sees a purpose. Not that suffering is pleasant, or that it comes with an explanation at the time. But it was aimed, and the target was his self-reliance. Paul had every resource: training, languages, courage, intellect. A man with resources will use them and may never find out what God can do when they run out.

God who raises the dead. Not the God who prevents death, or explains it, but who raises the dead. The second of the Eighteen Benedictions, prayed daily by Jews, blessed God who “gives life to the dead”. Abraham trusted the same God: “He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead” (Hebrews 11:19), the God “who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist” (Romans 4:17). If God can raise the dead, no situation is beyond him, and death itself is not the end of the story.

On a Tuesday. When the redundancy letter arrives, what do you reach for first: savings, contacts, a plan? None of these is wrong; God gave them. But if you have never been past the end of them, you may not yet know from experience whether the God you profess holds. Pray before you plan.

verseByVerse.quote: He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us. On him we have set our hope that he will deliver us again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He rescued us from so deadly a danger, and he will rescue us. We have fixed our hope on him that he will continue to rescue us.

Three tenses. Delivered, will deliver, will deliver again. Memory of past rescue becomes ground for future confidence. Samuel set up a stone and called it Ebenezer: “Till now the LORD has helped us” (1 Samuel 7:12).

What it does not mean. Not a promise that Paul would never die. He was eventually executed in Rome. The final deliverance is the resurrection, which is why God is named “who raises the dead”. Every rescue in this life is a foretaste of that one.

A textual note. Some manuscripts read “deadly perils” (plural), and some have “and delivers” instead of “and he will deliver”, or omit the middle clause. The ESV follows the strongest early evidence; the meaning stands.

On a Tuesday. Keep a written record of answered prayers and past rescues. On a bad day, read it.

verseByVerse.quote: You also must help us by prayer, so that many will give thanks on our behalf for the blessing granted us through the prayers of many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You also help us by praying for us. Then many people will give thanks on our behalf for the gracious gift God gave us in answer to the prayers of many.

Help by prayer. Synypourgeō, “work together under”, as if putting your shoulder under a load beside someone else. A church that thinks Paul weak is told that its prayers are part of how he survives.

Thanks is the goal. The purpose of the rescue is not only that Paul is saved but that many will give thanks. Answered prayer is aimed at worship.

On a Tuesday. An elderly woman who has never led anything prays every week for a missionary she has met once. Her prayers are a shoulder under the load. And churches that ask for prayer but never report the answers rob her of the thanksgiving.

For worship. Next time a prayer you joined in is answered, give thanks aloud with others. That is what the answer was for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–24 — The Yes of God in Christ and Paul’s Changed Plans
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul defends his integrity. His conscience is clear: he has dealt with them openly and sincerely, by God’s grace rather than clever technique, and his letters mean what they say. His critics say his changed travel plans prove he is unreliable. Paul answers by pointing to God’s faithfulness: the message he preached was not a mixture of yes and no, because every promise God has made is confirmed in Christ, and the church says its Amen to that. It is God who keeps them firm, who has anointed and sealed them and given the Spirit as a first instalment. Paul stayed away to spare them a painful confrontation, not to dominate them; he wants to serve their joy.
verseByVerse.theology:
“All the promises of God find their Yes in him” (v. 20) — This is the hermeneutical key to the entire OT: every promise — to Abraham, to Moses, to David, through the prophets — is fulfilled in Christ. This does not mean every OT text is directly about Jesus; it means the entire trajectory of divine promise reaches its destination in him. The “Amen” that believers add in worship is their ratification of what God has already declared: yes, it is so, in Christ.

The Trinitarian shape of vv. 21–22 is worth noting: God establishes (the Father), anointed (chrisas — sharing the root with Christos), and sealed with the Spirit, giving the Spirit as a deposit (arrabōn — the down payment guaranteeing the full inheritance, as in Eph. 1:14). The three persons are active together in the believer’s assurance.
verseByVerse.examples: A church member accuses her pastor of inconsistency when he changes a ministry plan he had announced. He is tempted to defend himself by cataloguing the reasons. This passage suggests a different approach: the goal is not to vindicate the decision but to demonstrate that the change came from genuine care for those affected — the same reason Paul stayed away from Corinth. Integrity is not the absence of changed plans; it is the transparent, godly motivation behind all decisions, including the changes.

verseByVerse.quote: For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you. For we are not writing to you anything other than what you read and understand and I hope you will fully understand— just as you did partially understand us—that on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is what we are proud of: our conscience tells us that we have lived in the world, and especially in our dealings with you, with simplicity and godly sincerity, relying not on worldly wisdom but on the grace of God. We are not writing anything you cannot read and understand. I hope you will come to understand fully, as you have partly understood us already, that on the day of our Lord Jesus you can be proud of us, just as we will be proud of you.

The charge. Behind these verses lies an accusation: Paul is two-faced, says one thing in letters and another in person, hides his real motives (10:1, 10). His defence is his conscience before God.

Sincerity. Eilikrineia, traditionally explained as “tested by sunlight”: something held up to the light and found without flaw. Nothing hidden.

Not by earthly wisdom. Corinth prized rhetoric, the clever speech that could win an audience whatever the truth. Paul refused those techniques (1 Corinthians 2:1–5). Grace, not spin.

Nothing between the lines. His letters mean what they say. No hidden agenda.

Mutual boasting. On the last day, he will be their pride and they his. Even a strained relationship is held in the light of that day.

A textual note. Manuscripts divide between “simplicity” (haplotēti, ESV and KJV) and “holiness” (hagiotēti, found in the earliest papyrus and several major manuscripts, and preferred by some editors and by the RSV). The two words look alike in Greek. Either way, the point is the same: an undivided, transparent life.

On a Tuesday. Could your emails, contracts and promises be held up to the light? Write so that nothing needs reading between the lines.

verseByVerse.quote: Because I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second experience of grace. I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on my way to Judea. Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because I was confident of this, I planned to visit you first, so that you could have a double blessing. I meant to visit you on the way to Macedonia and come back to you from Macedonia, and have you send me on my way to Judea. Was I being fickle when I planned this? Or do I make my plans like a worldly person, ready to say both “Yes, yes” and “No, no”?

The travel plans. In 1 Corinthians 16:5–7 Paul said he would come through Macedonia and then to Corinth. Later he told them of a better plan: Corinth, Macedonia, Corinth again, then Judea with the collection for the poor. Then, after the painful visit, he cancelled the return and sent a letter instead. His critics said: he cannot even keep his word about a journey; why trust his gospel?

Second grace. Two visits, two blessings. Paul thought of visiting as giving.

According to the flesh. A worldly planner says yes and no in the same breath, keeping his options open, saying whatever suits him at the time.

A textual note. A few manuscripts read “a second joy” (charan) instead of “a second grace” (charin). The words differ by one letter. “Grace” is better attested and fits Paul’s thought.

What it does not mean. Not that a Christian can never change plans. Paul changed his, for good reasons (v. 23). Integrity is not never changing your mind; it is never being double-minded.

On a Tuesday. If you have to cancel or change something you promised, explain why honestly and soon. Do not let people find out.
verseByVerse.note: Paul had changed his travel plans, and some at Corinth accused him of being unreliable.

verseByVerse.quote: As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes. For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As surely as God is faithful, our word to you is not “Yes” and “No” at once. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom Silas, Timothy and I preached among you, was not “Yes” and “No”; in him it has always been “Yes”. For no matter how many promises God has made, they are “Yes” in Christ. And so through him the “Amen” is spoken by us to the glory of God.

From travel plans to the gospel. Paul moves from the small to the vast. God is faithful; his Son is God’s great “Yes”; so the message about him is not unreliable, whatever Paul’s diary looks like.

Silvanus. Silas, Paul’s companion on the second journey, who preached with Timothy when the church was founded (Acts 18:5).

Every promise. To Abraham a seed and a blessing for the nations; to David a king for ever; through the prophets a new covenant, a new heart, the Spirit poured out, the dead raised. All of them come true in Christ. This is a key to reading the Old Testament: not that every verse is directly about Jesus, but that every promise finds its destination in him (Luke 24:27, 44).

Amen. A Hebrew word meaning “firm, true, so be it”. God says “Yes” in Christ; we say “Amen” to it in worship. Jesus himself is called “the Amen, the faithful and true witness” (Revelation 3:14). Isaiah 65:16 calls God, literally, “the God of Amen” (ESV “the God of truth”).

On a Tuesday. Write down one promise of God that you need this week (Romans 8:28; Hebrews 13:5; Isaiah 41:10). Then say “Amen” to it, aloud, through Christ.

For worship. Every “Amen” in church is the congregation signing its name under God’s promises. Say it like that.
verseByVerse.note: Silvanus is Silas, who worked with Paul at Corinth. “Amen” means “it is true, so be it.”

verseByVerse.quote: And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ, and has anointed us, and who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it is God who keeps us, together with you, standing firm in Christ. He anointed us, put his seal of ownership on us, and gave us his Spirit in our hearts as a down payment of what is to come.

Four verbs, all God’s. Establishes (bebaioō, a legal word for confirming a contract), anointed, sealed, gave the Spirit. The Father, the Son (Anointed One: chrisas is a pun on Christos) and the Spirit are all at work in the believer’s security.

Anointed. Kings, priests and prophets were anointed in Israel. Christ is the Anointed One. In him, all believers share his anointing: “you have been anointed by the Holy One” (1 John 2:20). Not a special class of clergy, but “us with you”.

Seal. A wax seal on a document or jar marked ownership, guaranteed contents and protected from tampering.

Guarantee. Arrabōn, a Semitic loan-word used in business for a deposit or first instalment, which pledged that the full payment would follow. In modern Greek arravōna means an engagement ring. The Spirit is the first part of heaven, given now, guaranteeing the rest (Ephesians 1:13–14; Romans 8:23).

When is the seal given? Some (classical Pentecostals, and in a different way Martyn Lloyd-Jones) taught that the sealing of the Spirit is a distinct experience after conversion, an assurance or baptism in the Spirit. Some sacramental traditions identify the seal with baptism or confirmation. Verdict: Paul says the believers “were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit” when they believed (Ephesians 1:13). The seal is the Spirit himself, given to every Christian at the beginning. Christians may later receive deeper assurance and fresh fillings of the Spirit, but no believer lacks the seal.

On a Tuesday. When you doubt whether you really belong to God, remember: your security rests on God’s four verbs, not on your feelings. The deposit has been paid.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership. The word for “guarantee” was used in business for a first instalment or deposit, pledging that the full payment will follow.

verseByVerse.quote: But I call God to witness against me—it was to spare you that I refrained from coming again to Corinth. Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy, for you stand firm in your faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I call on God as my witness, and stake my life on it: it was to spare you that I did not come back to Corinth. Not that we rule over your faith; we are working with you for your joy, because it is by faith you stand firm.

An oath. “Against my soul”: Paul stakes his life. When integrity is attacked, he calls on God, who sees motives.

To spare you. A third visit would have meant open discipline. He wrote instead, hoping they would put things right first (2:1–4; 13:2). Delay was mercy.

Not lords of your faith. An apostle, with real authority, refuses to dominate. Peter tells elders the same: “not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3). The Reformation principle: “God alone is Lord of the conscience” (Westminster Confession 20.2). No pastor, priest or church can command belief beyond what God’s word says.

Fellow workers for your joy. What a description of a pastor’s job. Not managers of their faith, but helpers of their joy.

On a Tuesday. If you lead anything in church, ask: do people come away from me feeling controlled or helped? And if you are tempted to give up a church because a leader overreached, remember that you stand by faith in Christ, not in them.

2.title: Forgiveness, the Aroma of Christ, and the Triumph of God
2.overview:
Paul continues to explain why he did not come back to Corinth. After the “painful visit”, in which one man publicly wronged him, he chose to write a tearful letter instead of returning to discipline them in person. The letter worked: the church disciplined the man. Now Paul’s concern is the opposite danger. The punishment has been enough. They must forgive him, comfort him and reaffirm their love, or Satan will take advantage, whether by crushing the man with excessive grief or by splitting the church.

Then Paul tells of his anxiety at Troas, where he could not wait for Titus’s news and left an open door to go to Macedonia. Before finishing the story (it resumes at 7:5), he bursts into thanks. God leads his servants in a Roman triumphal procession, captives of Christ on display, and through them spreads the fragrance of Christ everywhere: to some a smell of death, to others of life. Who is adequate for that? Not those who peddle God’s word for profit, but those who speak sincerely, as sent by God, in his sight.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Severe Letter and Forgiveness of the Offender
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul explains why he wrote a severe letter instead of making another painful visit: he did not want to grieve the very people who give him joy, and he wrote in anguish and tears, out of love. The man who caused the trouble has wronged the whole church, not just Paul, and the church has now disciplined him. That is enough. Paul urges them to forgive, comfort and openly welcome him back, so that he is not crushed by sorrow, and so that Satan does not exploit the situation. Their response will show whether they obey in everything, including restoration.
verseByVerse.theology: The passage teaches that church discipline has a defined goal: restoration, not condemnation. This is the consistent NT pattern: Matthew 18:15–20, Galatians 6:1, 1 Corinthians 5. Discipline protects the community and pursues the restoration of the erring member. When the discipline has achieved its purpose, continuing to withhold forgiveness becomes its own sin — a sin that Satan is actively happy to see, because it fractures the community and communicates to the world that the church’s gospel of forgiveness does not apply internally.
verseByVerse.examples: A church elder who was removed from office after a moral failure has spent two years in genuine repentance and restoration. The leadership has quietly re-engaged him in limited service; but a vocal minority insists that any restoration is a betrayal of those he hurt. This passage does not minimise the hurt — Paul explicitly says the offender has caused grief to some extent (v. 5). But it insists that the goal of discipline is always restoration, and that the refusal to forgive when repentance is genuine is not faithfulness; it is a gift to the enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: For I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you. For if I cause you pain, who is there to make me glad but the one whom I have pained?
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I made up my mind that I would not make another painful visit to you. For if I cause you pain, who is left to cheer me up except the very people I have hurt?

The painful visit. Acts does not record it. After writing 1 Corinthians, Paul made a short emergency trip from Ephesus to Corinth, and it went badly (12:14; 13:1–2 speak of a coming “third” visit). Someone attacked him openly, and the church did not stand with him.

Why not go back? Another visit would have meant another confrontation. Paul’s joy is bound up with them. Hurting them would hurt himself.

What it does not mean. Paul is not avoiding conflict. He wrote a stern letter instead (v. 4) and will come with authority if he must (13:2). He chose the route most likely to bring repentance.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes the wise thing after a blow-up with a family member or colleague is not to rush back into the room, but to write carefully, pray, and give time.
verseByVerse.note: This painful visit is not recorded in Acts; it came between 1 and 2 Corinthians.

verseByVerse.quote: And I wrote as I did, so that when I came I might not suffer pain from those who should have made me rejoice, for I felt sure of all of you, that my joy would be the joy of you all. For I wrote to you out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears, not to cause you pain but to let you know the abundant love that I have for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I wrote to you as I did so that, when I came, I would not be made sad by the people who ought to make me glad. I was sure that my joy would be the joy of all of you. I wrote out of deep distress and anguish of heart, with many tears. I did not mean to hurt you, but to show you how much I love you.

Which letter? Christians have identified the “tearful letter” three ways.

1 Corinthians itself (the view of many older commentators). But 1 Corinthians does not read like a letter written in anguish and tears, and it deals with many matters, not one offender.

2 Corinthians 10–13, later attached to chapters 1–9. Those chapters are certainly severe. But they speak of a visit still to come and do not mention the offender.

A letter now lost. Paul wrote other letters to Corinth that we do not have (1 Corinthians 5:9).

Verdict: most likely a lost letter. God did not choose to preserve every letter Paul wrote, only those he inspired for the whole church.

Tears. A pastor who rebukes without tears is dangerous. “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Proverbs 27:6). The severe letter was not a loss of temper; it was love with no other way left.

On a Tuesday. Before you send a hard email to an employee, a child or a church member, ask: would they be able to tell from it that I love them? If not, rewrite it, and perhaps pray over it overnight.
verseByVerse.note: This severe letter is probably lost; some think it is part of 2 Corinthians 10–13.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if anyone has caused pain, he has caused it not to me, but in some measure—not to put it too severely—to all of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone has caused grief, he has not grieved me alone, but to some degree, not to put it too strongly, all of you.

Who was he? Paul does not name him.

Many older commentators, from Chrysostom on, identified him with the man living with his father’s wife in 1 Corinthians 5.

Most modern scholars think he was someone who personally attacked Paul during the painful visit, perhaps a church member stirred up by the visiting teachers.

Verdict: the second fits better. Paul speaks of a wrong done to him (7:12) and of a punishment by majority vote, not the handing over to Satan of 1 Corinthians 5:5. Either way the principle is the same.

Not to me. Paul refuses to make it personal. A sin against a leader is a sin against the whole church, and he plays down his own hurt.

On a Tuesday. When you have been wronged in church, resist making yourself the centre of the story. Ask what the church as a whole needs.
verseByVerse.note: The offender is unnamed; he is most likely not the man disciplined in 1 Corinthians 5 but someone who had publicly opposed Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: For such a one, this punishment by the majority is enough, so you should rather turn to forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The punishment the majority has given this man is enough. Now, instead, you should forgive him and comfort him, or he may be swallowed up by too much grief.

Church discipline. The church had acted: “the majority” suggests a decision of the congregation, perhaps excluding him from fellowship (Matthew 18:15–17). Some may have wanted harsher measures; Paul says enough.

The goal is restoration. Discipline is never mere punishment. Its aim is repentance and return. “You who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness” (Galatians 6:1).

Overwhelmed. Katapinō: swallowed up, drowned. Too much sorrow can destroy as surely as too little. A man who repents and finds the door still shut may despair or harden.

What it does not mean. Not that forgiveness means pretending nothing happened, or putting an offender straight back into leadership or a position of trust. Forgiveness restores fellowship. Trust and office may need to be rebuilt over time, especially where there has been abuse; the safety of the vulnerable must come first.

On a Tuesday. When someone in your church has fallen badly and repented, be the first to sit next to them on Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: So I beg you to reaffirm your love for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I urge you to reaffirm your love for him publicly.

Reaffirm. Kyroō: to ratify, a legal word for formally confirming a decision. Just as the discipline was a public act of the church, so must the restoration be. Not a private word but an open welcome.

On a Tuesday. In families as well as churches: after a hard word or a punishment, make the reconciliation as visible as the rebuke was. A hug, a meal, a word in front of the others.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is why I wrote, that I might test you and know whether you are obedient in everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is why I wrote: to test you and see whether you would be obedient in everything.

The test. Dokimē: proven character, metal tested and found genuine. The severe letter was a test of whether they would deal with sin. They passed. Now comes the second test: will they forgive?

In everything. Obedience includes both discipline and restoration. A church that is good at one and bad at the other has failed half the test.

On a Tuesday. Are you better at confronting or at forgiving? Ask God for the one that comes harder.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive. Indeed, what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ, so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone you forgive, I forgive as well. And what I have forgiven, if there was anything for me to forgive, I have forgiven for your sake in the presence of Christ, so that Satan cannot outwit us. For we are well aware of his schemes.

In the presence of Christ. Literally “in the face of Christ”: before him, as he watches. The Latin Vulgate translated it in persona Christi, “in the person of Christ”, and Roman Catholic theology came to use that phrase for a priest acting in Christ’s place when he pronounces absolution. Verdict: the Greek means “before Christ’s face”, as in the ESV. Paul forgives as one accountable to Christ, not as standing in for him. Christ has given his church the authority to declare forgiveness to the repentant (John 20:23), but the church declares what God does; it does not do it in his place.

If I have forgiven anything. Paul plays down his personal injury again. He has no grudge to nurse.

Satan’s designs. Noēmata: plans, schemes (compare “the schemes of the devil”, Ephesians 6:11). Satan can use a church’s harshness as well as its laxity. Here the danger is unforgiveness: a man crushed, a church split, a gospel of grace contradicted by graceless people.

On a Tuesday. If you are holding a grudge against someone who has apologised, recognise that Satan wants it kept. Forgive them, “as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32), and tell them so.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul resumes the story of his journey. At Troas there was an open door for the gospel, but he was too anxious about Corinth to stay when Titus did not arrive, so he went on to Macedonia. Before telling what happened next, he breaks into thanks. He pictures God leading him as a captive in Christ’s victory parade, with the scent of the knowledge of Christ spreading wherever he goes. To some that scent means death, to others life. No one is adequate for such a task, but Paul, unlike those who sell a diluted message, speaks sincerely as one sent by God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The triumphal procession image is rich and theologically precise. In a Roman triumph, captives were led in chains behind the victor — some to be executed at the procession’s end, some to be enslaved. Paul’s use of the image for himself is deliberately surprising: the apostle is not the victorious general but a captive in Christ’s train. Yet this is not degradation — to be a captive of Christ, led in his triumph, is the highest possible dignity. The early church’s constant refrain — “slave of Christ” (doulos Christou) — captures the same paradox: absolute belonging to Christ is absolute dignity.

The double effect of the gospel (life to some, death to others) is grounded in passages like Isaiah 8:14 (the stone of stumbling) and Luke 2:34 (this child is set for the falling and rising of many). The gospel is not universally received, but this is not a failure of the gospel; it is a revelation of the human heart. The same sun that softens wax hardens clay — not because the sun changed but because the materials are different.
verseByVerse.examples: A missionary returns from several years in a largely unresponsive field and struggles with a sense of failure — very few converts, considerable opposition. This passage speaks to him directly: the task is not to produce results but to be the aroma of Christ. The spreading of the fragrance is the mission; the effect — life or death — belongs to God and to the hearts of those who encounter it. Faithfulness is measured by the aroma, not by the response.

verseByVerse.quote: When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ, even though a door was opened for me in the Lord, my spirit was not at rest because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ, the Lord opened a door for me. Even so, I could not rest in my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia.

The story. Paul had sent Titus to Corinth with the severe letter and arranged to meet him, probably at Troas, the port on the north-west coast of Asia Minor near ancient Troy. Titus did not come. If the sailing season was ending, Titus would have to come overland through Macedonia, so Paul went to meet him (7:5–7).

An open door, left. A real opportunity for the gospel (compare 1 Corinthians 16:9; Colossians 4:3). Paul left it because his heart was in Corinth. Paul was not a machine; the anxiety of 11:28 was real.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul was disobedient or lacked faith. An open door is an opportunity, not a command. Paul weighed it against pastoral duty to a church in crisis and chose the church. Sometimes the right choice is the smaller-looking one.

On a Tuesday. Restlessness over people you love is not always unbelief. Paul had it. Bring it to God, and sometimes, like Paul, go and find out.
verseByVerse.note: Troas was a port on the Aegean coast of Asia. Titus was a trusted Gentile co-worker, sent to Corinth with the severe letter.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us as his captives in a triumphal procession, and through us spreads everywhere the fragrance of knowing him.

A Roman triumph. When a general won a great victory, the Senate might grant him a triumph: a parade through Rome to the temple of Jupiter. The general rode in a chariot; behind or before him marched his soldiers, the spoils, and the captured enemy leaders in chains, often to be executed at the end. Incense and flowers filled the streets.

Victor or captive? Is Paul one of the victorious soldiers sharing the triumph (KJV: “causeth us to triumph”) or one of the captives?

The verb thriambeuō with a direct object means “to lead in triumph” as a captive. Paul uses it of the defeated powers: “by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15).

Verdict: captive. Paul, the former enemy of Christ, conquered on the Damascus road, is now displayed in Christ’s victory parade. That is why his weakness and suffering are not a contradiction of his apostleship but its proof. The Corinthians wanted a triumphant apostle; Paul says he is the conquered one in Christ’s triumph, and glad of it.

Fragrance. The incense of the procession. Wherever Paul goes, the knowledge of Christ spreads like a smell through the streets.

For worship. Thank God that he conquered you, and that being Christ’s captive is the only true freedom. “Make me a captive, Lord, and then I shall be free” (George Matheson).
verseByVerse.note: A Roman triumph was a victory parade through the city; captives were led in chains, and incense was burned along the route.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing, to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For to God we are the sweet smell of Christ, among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing. To the perishing, we are a deadly smell that leads to death; to those being saved, a life-giving fragrance that leads to life. And who is equal to such a task?

Two smells. To the victors in a triumph, the incense smelled of victory and celebration. To the prisoners, it smelled of death; they knew where the parade ended. The same smell, two meanings.

Aroma to God. First of all, the gospel and its messengers are a pleasing sacrifice to God, whatever people make of them (Ephesians 5:2).

Being saved, perishing. Present tenses: two groups on two roads. The gospel divides them. Simeon said of the infant Jesus, “this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel” (Luke 2:34). Jesus: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

What it does not mean. Not that preachers should judge success by results. The aroma is pleasing to God whether people accept it or not. Nor that God takes pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). The gospel is a real offer of life to all who hear; those who reject it harden themselves, and God gives them over to what they choose (Romans 1:24).

Who is sufficient? No one. The answer comes in 3:5–6: “our sufficiency is from God.”

On a Tuesday. When you share the gospel with a colleague and they mock it, you have not failed. You were the aroma of Christ to God. When another listens, it is God’s doing, not yours.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are not, like so many, peddlers of God’s word, but as men of sincerity, as commissioned by God, in the sight of God we speak in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are not like so many who peddle God’s word for profit. No, we speak in Christ as people of integrity, sent by God and speaking before God.

Peddlers. Kapēleuontes: a kapēlos was a small retailer or innkeeper, notorious for watering down wine and fiddling measures. Isaiah complained of “your best wine mixed with water” (Isaiah 1:22, in the Greek Old Testament with this same word family). The visiting teachers in Corinth charged fees and adjusted the message to please (11:7–20). Paul preached free and told the truth.

Sincerity. The same word as 1:12: held up to the light, no flaws.

From God, before God, in Christ. The source of the message (God sent him), the audience that matters (God sees him), and the sphere (union with Christ).

A textual note. A few early manuscripts, including the earliest papyrus, read “the rest” (loipoi) instead of “many” (polloi). That would mean all other preachers peddle the word, which is implausible. “Many” is the better reading.

What it does not mean. Not that it is wrong for preachers to be paid. Paul himself says “the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14). The sin is diluting the message for money or approval.

On a Tuesday. Any Christian who speaks about God (a Sunday school teacher, a writer, a parent) can water it down: leaving out sin, judgement or the cost of discipleship because it would lose the audience. Say it whole, before God.
verseByVerse.note: A peddler was a street trader known for watering down his wine to increase profits.

3.title: Letters of Recommendation, the New Covenant, and the Unveiled Face
3.overview:
The visiting teachers in Corinth carried letters of recommendation and probably claimed the authority of Moses. Paul answers both claims. He needs no letter: the Corinthians themselves are his letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts, just as God promised through Jeremiah and Ezekiel that the new covenant would write his law on hearts, not stone. His adequacy comes from God, who has made him a minister of that new covenant, “not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.”

Then Paul compares the two covenants through the story of Exodus 34. When Moses came down from Sinai with the law, his face shone so that Israel could not look at him, and he put on a veil. Paul argues: if the ministry that brought condemnation came with such glory, a glory that was being set aside, how much greater is the ministry of the Spirit and of righteousness, which lasts. To this day a veil lies over the hearts of those who read Moses without Christ; but whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. And all believers, with unveiled faces, behold the glory of the Lord and are being transformed into his image, from one degree of glory to another, by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Ministers of the New Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s rivals came with letters of recommendation. Paul needs none: the Corinthian church is his letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts rather than in ink or on stone, just as the prophets promised for the new covenant. His confidence rests not on his own ability but on God, who has made him a servant of that new covenant. The old covenant, written on stone, could only condemn; the Spirit gives life.
verseByVerse.theology: The contrast between letter and Spirit (v. 6) — “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” — is one of the most misunderstood phrases in Paul. It does not mean that the written word of Scripture is deadly and only spiritual illumination gives life (a Gnostic-leaning interpretation). In context, “the letter” refers specifically to the Mosaic law written on stone — the external commandment that makes demands it cannot empower fulfilling, that reveals sin it cannot remove. The Spirit gives life by doing what the letter could not: writing the law on the heart, enabling obedience from the inside. This is the Jeremiah 31/Ezekiel 36 promise in Paul’s theological shorthand.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation that prides itself on doctrinal correctness — its members can pass any biblical literacy test, articulate the five points of Calvinism, and explain every Confession — but whose relational life is cold and whose evangelistic impact is minimal. The letter/Spirit contrast is not a critique of doctrine or written Scripture; it is a diagnosis of the difference between external knowledge of the truth and inward transformation by it. The new covenant minister’s goal is not to fill heads but to be the instrument through whom the Spirit writes on hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are we starting to promote ourselves again? Or do we need, as some people do, letters of recommendation to you or from you?

Letters of recommendation. In the ancient world travellers carried letters from someone known, introducing them to people who did not know them. Christians used them too: the church at Ephesus wrote to welcome Apollos at Corinth (Acts 18:27), and Paul recommends Phoebe (Romans 16:1–2). The rival teachers in Corinth arrived with impressive letters, perhaps from Jerusalem, and asked the Corinthians for more.

Again. Paul has been accused of self-commendation, perhaps because of what he wrote in 1:12–14 or in 1 Corinthians. He is sensitive to it.

What it does not mean. Not that references are wrong. Paul writes them himself. The point is that his ministry among them needs none: they know him.

On a Tuesday. CVs, references and credentials have their place. But the best reference a parent, teacher or pastor can have is the people they have served.
verseByVerse.note: Letters of recommendation were common for travellers; Paul’s rivals at Corinth came with them.

verseByVerse.quote: You yourselves are our letter of recommendation, written on our hearts, to be known and read by all. And you show that you are a letter from Christ delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts, known and read by everybody. You make it clear that you are a letter from Christ, which we delivered, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on the tablets of human hearts.

A living letter. The Corinthian church is Paul’s reference. Their changed lives (1 Corinthians 6:9–11: idolaters, thieves and drunkards washed and made holy) are open for anyone in the city to read.

A letter from Christ. Christ is the author; Paul is the courier; the Spirit is the ink.

Stone and heart. The background is two prophecies. The law was written on tablets of stone at Sinai (Exodus 31:18). God promised a new covenant: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33); “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put my Spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26–27). Paul says this has happened in Corinth.

A textual note. Most manuscripts read “written on our hearts”; a few important ones (including Sinaiticus) read “your hearts”, which seems to fit the logic better. “Our” is far better attested, and makes sense: Paul carries the Corinthians in his heart (7:3) as his letter of recommendation wherever he goes.

On a Tuesday. Your neighbours may never read a Bible. They read you. What would they learn about Christ from your week?

parallels.desc: tablets of stone, written with the finger of God
a heart of flesh

verseByVerse.quote: Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God. Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have this kind of confidence before God through Christ. Not that we are competent in ourselves to claim that anything comes from us. Our competence comes from God.

Sufficient. Hikanos: adequate, competent, qualified. The answer to the question of 2:16, “Who is sufficient for these things?” Not Paul in himself, but God in him.

Confidence, not self-confidence. Paul is bold (3:12) but not proud. The confidence is “through Christ” and “toward God”.

On a Tuesday. When you feel inadequate to visit someone grieving, teach a class or speak to a colleague about Christ, you are right. Then remember: “our sufficiency is from God.” Go anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has made us competent to serve a new covenant, not one of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

The new covenant. Jeremiah 31:31–34. Jesus at the Last Supper: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). Its marks: the law written on hearts, everyone knowing God, sins forgiven and remembered no more.

Letter and Spirit. What does “the letter” mean?

Origen and many after him read it as the literal sense of Scripture, contrasted with a deeper spiritual or allegorical sense. This became a major principle of medieval interpretation.

The Reformers and most modern interpreters read “the letter” as the law written on stone, given from outside, demanding obedience but not giving the power to obey.

Verdict: the second. The contrast is stone tablets and Spirit-written hearts (v. 3), not literal and allegorical readings. This verse is no warrant for ignoring the plain sense of Scripture.

The letter kills. Not because the law is bad. “The law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good” (Romans 7:12). But to a sinner, a perfect law with no power to change him can only condemn. “The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me” (Romans 7:10).

Does the law still matter for Christians? Antinomians have used this verse to set aside the moral law entirely. The Reformed view: the law cannot justify, but it still shows us God’s will, and the Spirit now writes that same law on our hearts so that we love to keep it (Romans 8:4). Verdict: the Spirit does not abolish God’s moral law; he gives the life to keep it.

On a Tuesday. If you try to make yourself good by a list of rules, you will either fail and despair, or succeed and become proud. Ask for the Spirit, who changes desires.
verseByVerse.note: The “letter” is the law written on stone, which could condemn but not give life.

parallels.desc: a new covenant

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–18 — The Fading Glory and the Surpassing Glory; the Unveiled Face
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul compares the two covenants through the story of Moses’ shining face. The law came with real glory, so bright that Israel could not look at Moses. But that ministry brought condemnation and was temporary. The ministry of the Spirit, which brings righteousness and lasts, has a far greater glory. Moses veiled his face; Paul speaks openly. A veil still lies over the hearts of those who read Moses without Christ, but it is removed whenever anyone turns to the Lord. The Lord meets us now by the Spirit, who brings freedom, and all believers, seeing his glory with unveiled faces, are being gradually changed into his likeness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Moses passage (Ex. 34) in Paul’s reading makes a claim that has been debated since the patristic period: Paul appears to say that Moses wore the veil to prevent the Israelites from seeing the glory’s end (v. 13), whereas Exodus dwells on the Israelites’ fear of his shining face. Paul is reading the text through the lens of its fulfilment in Christ: the entire Mosaic economy was a temporary arrangement pointing beyond itself, and the veil that covered Moses’s face symbolises the veil that covers the hearts of those who read him without recognising his Christological pointing.

The transformation passage (v. 18) is the key text for the Reformed understanding of sanctification as a work of the Spirit through the Word. Beholding — katoptrizomenoi (gazing as in a mirror, or reflecting as a mirror) — is the mechanism. The Word presents Christ; the Spirit uses the Word to produce in the believer the image they behold. John Owen, commenting on this verse, says that the primary means of sanctification is not moral effort but contemplation of the glory of Christ as revealed in the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: A spiritual director works with a young Christian who is exhausted by the effort of sanctification — constantly striving, measuring, failing, striving again. She introduces him to the practice of deliberate meditation on specific passages that describe the character and glory of Christ, asking him to rest in the image rather than immediately applying it. After several months he reports something shifting in his desires and responses — not through effort but through what this verse would call beholding. The transformation is from the Lord who is the Spirit; the means is the unveiled face gazing at glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its glory, which was being brought to an end, will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ministry that brought death, carved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not look at Moses’ face because of its brightness, though that glory was being set aside. How much more glorious, then, will the ministry of the Spirit be!

Exodus 34. When Moses came down Sinai the second time with the tablets, “Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God” (Exodus 34:29). The people “were afraid to come near him” (34:30). So he veiled his face when speaking to them, and removed it when he went in to speak with the LORD.

The ministry of death. A shocking phrase for the law. Not because it was evil, but because its effect on sinners was condemnation and death (Romans 7:9–11). Yet even it came with glory. Paul does not despise the old covenant.

Fading or being set aside? Katargoumenēn. Some translations say “fading” (RSV, NIV 1984). Exodus does not say Moses’ face faded. Paul’s word, used often by him, means “to render inoperative, abolish, bring to an end” (as in 3:11, 13, 14). Verdict: the glory was “being brought to an end” (ESV), meaning the whole old covenant arrangement was temporary, pointing beyond itself to Christ.

Lesser to greater. A Jewish argument form (qal wa-ḥomer): if this, how much more that.

On a Tuesday. If you were raised under a religion of rules (any religion, or a strict Christian upbringing), do not despise it all. Some of it was glory. But Christ is far more.

parallels.desc: the skin of Moses’ face shone

verseByVerse.quote: For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, the ministry of righteousness must far exceed it in glory. Indeed, in this case, what once had glory has come to have no glory at all, because of the glory that surpasses it. For if what was being brought to an end came with glory, much more will what is permanent have glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the ministry that condemns had glory, the ministry that brings righteousness overflows with far more glory. In fact, what once had glory has no glory now, in comparison with the glory that surpasses it. For if what was being brought to an end came with glory, much greater is the glory of what remains.

Condemnation and righteousness. The law declares guilty; the gospel declares righteous, because of Christ (5:21). The new covenant does not just demand righteousness; it gives it.

No glory at all. Like a candle beside the sun. The candle is still burning; it just cannot be seen.

Temporary and permanent. The old covenant was meant to last until Christ (Galatians 3:24–25). The new is “what is permanent”: there will be no third covenant.

How the covenants relate. Covenant theology (the Reformed view) sees one covenant of grace running through history: in the Old Testament under types and shadows, in the New in Christ. The Mosaic covenant was a temporary administration within it. Dispensationalists see sharper breaks between distinct ages. Verdict: covenant theology fits Paul. He contrasts the Mosaic ministry with the new, but grounds both in God’s one purpose and promises (1:20; Galatians 3:17).

For worship. Sing of the glory of the gospel: you were condemned and are now declared righteous. That is a greater glory than Moses’ shining face.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have such a hope, we are very bold, not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face so that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, since we have such a hope, we speak very boldly. We are not like Moses, who used to put a veil over his face so that the Israelites would not watch the end of what was passing away.

Boldness. Parrēsia: openness, plain speaking, nothing hidden. A free citizen’s right to speak freely. Paul hides nothing; he has an unfading message.

Why the veil? Exodus 34 says the people were afraid. Paul adds a further meaning: the veil kept Israel from seeing that the glory was temporary. He is not accusing Moses of deceit, but reading the veil as a sign that Israel was not yet able to see where the old covenant was heading.

On a Tuesday. Be open about your faith. You have nothing to hide and nothing that will fade.

parallels.desc: he put a veil over his face

verseByVerse.quote: But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains unlifted, because only through Christ is it taken away. Yes, to this day whenever Moses is read a veil lies over their hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But their minds were hardened. To this very day, when the old covenant is read, the same veil remains; it is not lifted, because only in Christ is it removed. Yes, to this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts.

Hardened. Pōroō: to petrify, to form a callus. A heart of stone, matching the tablets of stone (v. 3).

The veil moves. First it was on Moses’ face. Now it lies over the hearts of the hearers. The problem is not in the text but in the reader.

When Moses is read. Every Sabbath in the synagogue the law was read aloud (Acts 15:21). Paul, a former Pharisee, had sat through it for years without seeing Christ. Only on the Damascus road did the veil come off.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is a closed book for Christians or that Jews are uniquely blind. All of us, Gentiles too, are blind until God opens our eyes (4:4–6). And not that God has finished with Israel; Paul expects a future turning of many Jews to Christ: “And in this way all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:26).

On a Tuesday. Pray for Jewish friends and neighbours, with love and without arrogance. Christ was a Jew, and the veil can lift.
verseByVerse.note: “Moses” here means the books of Moses, read aloud each Sabbath in the synagogue.

verseByVerse.quote: But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But whenever a person turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.

Echo of Exodus. “Whenever Moses went in before the LORD to speak with him, he would remove the veil, until he came out” (Exodus 34:34). Paul makes it a pattern for everyone: turn to the Lord as Moses did, and the veil comes off.

Turns. Epistrephō: the word for conversion (Acts 9:35; 1 Thessalonians 1:9).

Who removes it? The verb is passive: “is removed”, by God. We turn, but God lifts the veil. Jesus “opened their minds to understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45).

On a Tuesday. When you read the Bible and it seems closed, turn to the Lord. Pray before you read: “Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18).
verseByVerse.note: Paul echoes Exodus: whenever Moses went in before the LORD, he removed the veil.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now “the Lord” in that passage means the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.

The Lord is the Spirit. What does this mean?

Some have taken it to mean Christ and the Spirit are the same person, which would deny the Trinity.

Most take Paul to be explaining the Exodus text he has just quoted: the “Lord” to whom Moses turned, and to whom we turn, is now encountered as the Spirit, who applies the new covenant to us.

Verdict: the second. Paul at once distinguishes them: “the Spirit of the Lord”. He is not merging persons but saying that the Lord of Exodus is present now by the Spirit. The Father, Son and Spirit are one God, and to meet the Spirit is to meet the Lord.

Freedom. From the veil, from condemnation, from the law as a way of earning life, from fear. Freedom to see and to approach God. “For freedom Christ has set us free” (Galatians 5:1).

What it does not mean. Not freedom to do whatever we like. “Do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh” (Galatians 5:13). Nor does it mean that worship led by the Spirit must be unstructured. It means freedom from the veil, not freedom from order (1 Corinthians 14:33, 40).

On a Tuesday. Are you living as if under the old veil, afraid of God, hiding from him, trying to earn approval? The Spirit sets you free to come to him as a child.

verseByVerse.quote: And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all of us, with faces unveiled, gazing at the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are being changed into the same image, from one degree of glory to the next. This comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.

We all. Not just Moses, the prophet, but every believer has unveiled access to God’s glory.

Beholding as in a mirror. Katoptrizomenoi can mean “beholding as in a mirror” or “reflecting like a mirror”. Ancient mirrors were polished bronze, giving a real but imperfect image (1 Corinthians 13:12). Verdict: “beholding” (ESV). The context is about seeing, as Moses saw God. We see the Lord’s glory in the gospel (4:4–6), and become like what we look at.

Transformed. Metamorphoumetha, the word used of Jesus’ transfiguration (Mark 9:2) and of renewing the mind (Romans 12:2). Present tense: it is happening now, gradually.

The same image. The image of Christ, “the image of God” (4:4). God’s plan is that we be “conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29), restoring the image damaged in Adam.

Is this deification? Eastern Orthodox theology speaks of theosis: believers becoming “partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4). Orthodox theologians do not mean becoming God in essence, but sharing in God’s life and energies. Verdict: the Reformed view prefers the language of conformity to Christ and union with him. We share God’s holiness and life by grace, but always remain creatures. The image we are changed into is Christ’s, not God’s essence.

Degree to degree. Sanctification is gradual, not instant: a slow glory, often more visible to others than to ourselves.

On a Tuesday. We become like what we look at. If your attention is on the news, your phone and your grievances, you will become like them. Spend time looking at Christ in the gospels. Change will come slowly, and others may notice before you do.

For worship. Charles Wesley: “Changed from glory into glory, till in heaven we take our place, till we cast our crowns before thee, lost in wonder, love and praise.”
