4.title: Treasure in Jars of Clay
4.overview:
Paul has described the surpassing glory of the new covenant ministry. Now he faces the obvious objection: if the ministry is so glorious, why is the minister so unimpressive, so beaten up, so weak? The Corinthians, living in a city that admired polish, power and success, were embarrassed by an apostle who looked like a failure.

Paul answers in three movements. First, he does not lose heart or use tricks; he openly states the truth. If some cannot see it, it is because Satan, “the god of this world”, has blinded them, while the God who said “Let light shine out of darkness” has shone into believers’ hearts with the light of his glory in the face of Christ. Second, this treasure is kept in clay jars, cheap and fragile, so that everyone can see the power is God’s. Paul is afflicted but not crushed, perplexed but not in despair, struck down but not destroyed; he carries Jesus’ death in his body so that Jesus’ life may appear. Third, he does not lose heart, because although his outer self is wasting away, his inner self is renewed daily, and this light, momentary affliction is producing an eternal weight of glory. So he looks not at what is seen, which is temporary, but at what is unseen, which is eternal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Light Shining in Darkness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because his ministry is a gift of mercy, Paul does not give up, and he refuses tricks or distortion of God’s word, relying on open truth. If some cannot see the gospel, it is because Satan has blinded them. Paul preaches Christ as Lord, not himself, and regards himself as their servant. Conversion is God’s work, like creation: the God who first commanded light has shone into believers’ hearts so that they see his glory in the face of Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The identification of Christ as “the image of God” (v. 4) is one of Paul’s most direct Christological statements, paralleled in Colossians 1:15. Christ is not merely like God or a representative of God; he is the very image — the precise visible representation — of the invisible God. To see Christ is to see God (John 14:9). The glory of God is concentrated in the face of Jesus Christ (v. 6) — not in theophanies or visions or mystical experiences, but in the specific person of Jesus of Nazareth, crucified and risen.

The parallel between Gen. 1:3 (“Let there be light”) and v. 6 (“God who said Let light shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts”) is one of the NT’s most striking statements about the nature of conversion: it is a creative act of God, analogous to the original creation. Regeneration is not human spiritual development; it is the same divine fiat that created light from nothing. This is the Reformers’ point: regeneration precedes and enables faith; it is not faith that produces the new birth but the new birth that produces faith.
verseByVerse.examples: A campus minister explains the gospel to a sharp philosophy student who has engaged with every argument and remains unconvinced. He is tempted to find a better argument. This passage suggests a different diagnosis: the issue may not be intellectual but spiritual — a blinding that no amount of superior argument can overcome. The appropriate response includes not abandoning the argument (Paul commends himself to the conscience) but adding sustained prayer for the God who speaks light into darkness to do so in this particular darkness.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, having this ministry by the mercy of God, we do not lose heart. But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. We refuse to practice cunning or to tamper with God’s word, but by the open statement of the truth we would commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, since we have this ministry because God has shown us mercy, we do not give up. We have rejected secret and shameful methods. We do not use trickery, and we do not distort God’s word. Instead, by stating the truth openly, we commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in God’s sight.

By mercy. Paul, a former persecutor, never forgot that his ministry was a gift of mercy (1 Timothy 1:12–16). A man who knows he does not deserve his job is less likely to quit it over hardship.

We do not lose heart. Ouk enkakoumen: we do not become discouraged, give in, lose nerve. It frames the chapter (v. 16).

Underhanded ways. Corinth was used to orators who would say anything to win. “Cunning” (panourgia) is the craftiness of a con man. “Tamper with” (doloō) was used of adulterating wine or gold. The rival teachers were apparently accusing Paul of the very things they practised (12:16).

Open statement. Paul’s method: say the truth plainly and let conscience judge. No manipulation, no emotional pressure, no hidden agenda.

On a Tuesday. Sharing the gospel with a friend does not need technique. It needs honesty: say what is true, plainly, kindly, and let God work on their conscience.

verseByVerse.quote: And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And even if our gospel is hidden behind a veil, it is veiled only to those who are perishing. The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers so that they cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.

The veil again. From chapter 3. If people cannot see the gospel, the fault is not in the message or the messenger.

The god of this world. Literally “the god of this age”, meaning the present evil age (Galatians 1:4). Who is it?

Some early church writers (Irenaeus, Tertullian, Chrysostom), wanting to avoid the heretic Marcion’s idea of two gods, read it as the true God: “God has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this world.”

Almost all interpreters since take it as Satan, whom Jesus called “the ruler of this world” (John 12:31) and Paul “the prince of the power of the air” (Ephesians 2:2).

Verdict: Satan. He is not a god in reality, but he is treated as one by those who serve him, and “the whole world lies in the power of the evil one” (1 John 5:19). His power is real but limited and already broken (Colossians 2:15).

Blinded. Unbelief is not just a lack of information but spiritual blindness. Argument alone cannot cure it; only God can (v. 6).

Image of God. Christ is the exact representation of God (Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:3). To see the glory of Christ is to see the glory of God.

On a Tuesday. When a friend cannot see the gospel however clearly you explain it, do not despair or push harder. Pray that God will open their eyes. And keep explaining; it is through the message that God shines.
verseByVerse.note: “The god of this world” is Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we do not proclaim ourselves. We proclaim Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants because of Jesus.

Not ourselves. The visiting teachers were promoting themselves: their credentials, eloquence and visions. Paul preaches Christ.

Jesus Christ as Lord. The earliest Christian confession (Romans 10:9; Philippians 2:11). In a city with many lords (1 Corinthians 8:5), there is one.

Your slaves. Doulous. Christ is Lord; Paul is the Corinthians’ slave, for Jesus’ sake. Not because they are his masters, but because his Master serves them through him.

On a Tuesday. In any Christian service, ask whose name you want remembered. A youth leader can make the group about himself; a mother can make the family about her. Point beyond yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness”, is the one who has shone in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of God’s glory in the face of Jesus Christ.

Creation. “And God said, ‘Let there be light’” (Genesis 1:3). Also perhaps Isaiah 9:2: “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.” Conversion is a new creation (5:17). God does for the dark heart what he did for the dark world: he speaks, and there is light.

Damascus. Paul is surely remembering “a light from heaven, brighter than the sun” (Acts 26:13). But he says “our hearts”: what happened to him outwardly happens to every believer inwardly.

In the face of Jesus Christ. Moses saw God’s glory and his face shone (chapter 3). We see God’s glory in Christ’s face: in his life, death and resurrection, as told in the gospel.

Monergism. Who makes a person see? Not the person. As God alone created light, God alone gives spiritual sight. This is the Reformed doctrine of effectual calling (Westminster Confession 10.1).

A textual note. Some important early manuscripts read “the face of Christ”, others “Jesus Christ” or “Christ Jesus”. The meaning is unaffected.

For worship. If you see the glory of God in Christ at all, it is because God said “Let there be light” in you. Thank him for your conversion as you would for creation.

parallels.desc: let there be light

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — Treasure in Jars of Clay
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The treasure of the gospel is carried in fragile, ordinary containers, so that the power is clearly God’s. Paul describes his life as a series of near-defeats that never become defeats: pressed but not crushed, bewildered but not without hope, hunted but not abandoned, knocked down but not destroyed. He shares Jesus’ dying so that Jesus’ life can be seen in him, and his suffering brings life to others. Like the psalmist, he believes and therefore speaks, sure that the God who raised Jesus will raise him too. All of it serves the spread of grace and the increase of thanks to God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The four contrasts in vv. 8–9 are not merely biographical observations; they are a theological programme. The pattern of affliction-but-not-destroyed is the pattern of the cross applied to the messengers of the cross. The phrase rendered “the death of Jesus” (v. 10) uses a noun that means the process of dying, death-at-work, rather than the event. Paul is not saying that he dies as Jesus died, but that the same dying-of-Jesus that produced life for the world is at work in Paul’s ministry, producing life for the churches. The apostle’s weakness and suffering is the medium through which resurrection life is communicated. It is worth noting the honesty of v. 8: the verb behind “driven to despair” is the very word Paul used of himself in 1:8, where he says he despaired of life itself. He is describing the normal condition, not issuing an absolute guarantee.

Verse 13 — “I believed, and so I spoke” — quotes Psalm 116:10 in the Greek Old Testament, the psalm of a man who faced death and was delivered, who then declared that he believed and therefore spoke. Paul applies the psalm to the apostolic situation: even in the face of death, the minister speaks because he believes, and the faith of the psalmist and the faith of the Christian are shown to be one and the same pneuma. The resurrection of Jesus (v. 14) grounds this confidence — the same God who raised Jesus will raise us, and bring us with you into his presence.
verseByVerse.examples: A senior pastor of a large church steps down due to a serious health diagnosis and is replaced by a younger, more energetic successor. He struggles with the sense that his fragility is a disqualification. This chapter is addressed precisely to him: the jar of clay is not a disqualification from ministry; it is the precondition for God’s power being unambiguously visible. The question is not whether his vessel is strong enough but whether the treasure is still present — and treasure in a cracked jar leaks light rather than hiding it.

verseByVerse.quote: But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we keep this treasure in clay jars, to make it clear that this extraordinary power belongs to God, not to us.

Jars of clay. Cheap, everyday pottery, like a plastic bucket today. Corinth was famous for its pottery. Clay jars held everything from oil to grain and, when broken, were thrown away. Small clay oil lamps were also common. Valuables were sometimes hidden in clay jars; the Dead Sea Scrolls were found that way.

Gideon? Some hear an echo of Gideon’s men, who hid torches in jars, then broke them so the light blazed out (Judges 7:16–20). Whether Paul intended it or not, the picture fits: the jar must break for the light to be seen.

The treasure. The light of the knowledge of God’s glory in Christ (v. 6): the gospel.

To show. The purpose: if the container were impressive, people would credit the container. God puts priceless treasure in ordinary people so that the power is plainly his. The Corinthians wanted a golden vase of an apostle. God sent a clay pot.

On a Tuesday. Your weakness, ordinariness, lack of eloquence or chronic illness is not an obstacle to God using you. It may be the reason he chose you. A shy accountant who stammers when he prays aloud, but faithfully brings colleagues to church events, is a clay jar with treasure in it.
verseByVerse.note: Clay jars were cheap, fragile, everyday containers.

verseByVerse.quote: We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are hard pressed on every side, but not crushed; at a loss, but not utterly at a loss; hunted, but never abandoned; knocked down, but not knocked out.

Four pairs. Each first half is real. Each second half is God’s limit.

Afflicted, not crushed: pressed in a tight place, but not squeezed to nothing.

Perplexed, not driven to despair: a wordplay (aporoumenoi, exaporoumenoi): at a loss, but not totally at a loss. Not that he always knows what God is doing, but he is never left with no way at all. (Compare 1:8, where he did despair of life: not of God.)

Persecuted, not forsaken: chased by men, never deserted by God (Hebrews 13:5).

Struck down, not destroyed: perhaps a wrestling or battlefield image. Thrown down, not killed. Paul was stoned and left for dead at Lystra, then got up and walked back into the city (Acts 14:19–20).

On a Tuesday. Being perplexed is not failure. Many Christians are at a loss: a child’s illness with no explanation, a marriage they cannot fix. Paul was too. The promise is not understanding, but not being abandoned.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay: “perplexed” (aporoumenoi) but not “driven to despair” (exaporoumenoi) — at a loss, but not utterly at a loss.

verseByVerse.quote: always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We always carry around in our bodies the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be seen in our bodies. For we who are alive are always being handed over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus may be seen in our mortal flesh.

The dying of Jesus. Nekrōsis: the process of dying, not just death. Paul’s beatings, exhaustion and dangers (11:23–28) are a constant sharing in Jesus’ dying. He bears “on my body the marks of Jesus” (Galatians 6:17).

The life of Jesus. The risen life of Christ, shown now in Paul’s endurance, survival and joy, and fully at the resurrection (v. 14).

Given over. Paradidometha, the word used of Jesus being handed over to death (Romans 4:25; Mark 9:31). Paul’s life follows his Lord’s.

What it does not mean. Not that suffering itself is good or should be sought. Paul did not seek beatings. He accepted what came “for Jesus’ sake”. Nor is it only for apostles: every Christian is called to “take up his cross daily” (Luke 9:23).

On a Tuesday. A Christian carer, worn out with nights up for a disabled child, is carrying the dying of Jesus. Neighbours who see her patience are seeing the life of Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: So death is at work in us, but life in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So death is at work in us, but life is at work in you.

The exchange. Paul’s sufferings bring spiritual life to the Corinthians. This is the pattern of Christ himself, who died that others might live.

A hint of irony? Some hear a touch of irony: the Corinthians are comfortable and think themselves spiritually rich (1 Corinthians 4:8–13), while Paul suffers. But mainly it is a statement of how ministry works.

On a Tuesday. Parents, teachers, missionaries and pastors often spend themselves so that others flourish. That is not waste. It is the gospel pattern.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, “I believed, and so I spoke,” we also believe, and so we also speak, knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and bring us with you into his presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scripture says, “I believed, and therefore I spoke.” We have that same spirit of faith; we too believe, and therefore we speak, because we know that the one who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and bring us, together with you, into his presence.

Psalm 116. Paul quotes the Greek version of Psalm 116:10 (115:1 in the Greek numbering). The Hebrew reads differently (“I believed, even when I spoke: ‘I am greatly afflicted’”), but the context is the same: a psalm of a man rescued from death, who keeps faith in affliction and speaks of God’s deliverance. “The snares of death encompassed me” (116:3). Paul takes the psalmist’s experience as his own.

The same spirit. Possibly the Holy Spirit who gives faith, or the same attitude of faith as the psalmist. The first is likely: the Spirit is the source of faith (1 Corinthians 12:3, 9).

We believe, so we speak. Faith cannot keep quiet. Paul does not stop preaching because of suffering; his faith in the resurrection drives him on.

Raise us with Jesus. Our resurrection is guaranteed by his (1 Corinthians 15:20). “With” means united with him.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (KJV “by Jesus”) read “through Jesus”. The earliest read “with Jesus”. “With” is original.

On a Tuesday. If you believe Christ is risen, say so. Tell someone this week why you have hope when facing death.
verseByVerse.note: Paul quotes the Greek form of the psalm.

parallels.desc: I believed, even when I spoke

verseByVerse.quote: For it is all for your sake, so that as grace extends to more and more people it may increase thanksgiving, to the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this is for your benefit, so that as grace reaches more and more people it may make thanksgiving overflow to the glory of God.

For you. Paul’s sufferings, preaching and hope are for the church.

Grace, thanks, glory. The chain: grace spreads to more people, more people give thanks, God is glorified. This is the purpose of the whole ministry (1:11).

For worship. Thank God by name for the people through whom grace reached you: the person who first explained the gospel, the friend who prayed. That is part of the overflow.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–18 — The Outer and Inner; the Seen and Unseen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So Paul does not lose heart. His body is wearing out, but his inner life is renewed daily. Present troubles, heavy as they are, are light and brief beside the lasting glory they are preparing. So he keeps his attention on what cannot yet be seen, because the visible things are temporary and the unseen ones eternal.
verseByVerse.theology: The seen/unseen contrast (v. 18) is not Platonic dualism — Paul is not saying that the material world is bad and the spiritual world is good, or that the body is a prison from which the soul escapes. He is making an eschatological point: what is currently visible (the suffering, the wasting body, the opposition) is temporary; what is currently invisible (the renewed inner person, the weight of glory being prepared) is permanent. The resurrection of the body (ch. 5; 1 Cor. 15) will make the invisible visible — the glory will become physical and permanent in the resurrection.
verseByVerse.examples: An elderly woman in a nursing home, her body failing, tells her pastor that she has never felt closer to God. She cannot explain it; the outer self is clearly wasting away. But there is something else. This verse names what she is experiencing: while the outer is being destroyed, the inner is being renewed day by day. The renewal is not despite the physical decline but somehow through it — the loosening grip of the outer on the inner’s attention, the daily reminder that this is not home, the intensified gaze at the unseen.

verseByVerse.quote: So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we do not give up. Though our outward self is wearing out, our inner self is being renewed every day.

Outer and inner. The outer self is the body and our visible life in this world, subject to ageing, illness and death. The inner self is the person as God renews them, the life of the Spirit within (Romans 7:22; Ephesians 3:16).

What it does not mean. Not Plato’s idea that the body is a prison and only the soul matters. Paul believes in bodily resurrection (v. 14; 5:1–4). The human person is body and soul together (the dichotomist view; trichotomy, which divides spirit from soul, reads too much into a few verses). The point is that the visible decline is not the whole story.

Wasting away. Diaphtheiretai: being destroyed, wearing out. Paul says plainly what anyone over sixty knows.

Renewed day by day. Present tense, daily. Not a once-for-all experience but a steady renewal through the word, prayer and the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. A man with Parkinson’s, or a woman with dementia whose memory is going, is losing the outer self. Yet many such believers still sing hymns from memory and pray. Something inside is being renewed. For their carers: God is still at work in them when you cannot see it.

verseByVerse.quote: For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this slight and short-lived trouble is producing for us an eternal weight of glory, far beyond anything we can compare it with.

Light and momentary. From the man who lists his sufferings in 11:23–28: beatings, shipwreck, prison, hunger. “Light” only by comparison. “The sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us” (Romans 8:18).

Weight of glory. In Hebrew, “glory” (kabod) comes from a root meaning “heavy”. Paul, thinking in Hebrew, contrasts “light” affliction with “weight” of glory. Glory is not thin light but substantial, solid reality. C. S. Lewis’s famous sermon took this as its title.

Beyond all comparison. Kath’ hyperbolēn eis hyperbolēn: “excess to excess”, beyond all measure. Language breaks down.

Does suffering earn glory? Roman Catholic theology speaks of suffering as meritorious when united with Christ. Verdict: “preparing” (katergazetai) means producing or working out, not earning. Glory is a gift of grace. But God uses affliction to shape us for glory, and nothing endured for Christ is wasted (1 Peter 1:6–7).

On a Tuesday. Put your current trouble on the scales: a difficult year, a painful diagnosis. Then put eternity on the other side. Weigh them as Paul did.

For worship. Pray: “Lord, make my troubles light in my eyes by showing me the weight of the glory to come.”
verseByVerse.note: In Hebrew the word for “glory” comes from a root meaning “heavy” — glory has weight.

verseByVerse.quote: as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We do this by fixing our eyes not on what can be seen but on what cannot be seen. For what can be seen lasts only for a time, but what cannot be seen lasts for ever.

Look. Skopeō: to fix attention on, to aim at, like a runner watching the finishing line. The renewal of verse 16 happens as we look.

Seen and unseen. The seen: our bodies, troubles, possessions and the present world. The unseen: Christ, God, heaven, the resurrection, the coming glory. Moses “endured as seeing him who is invisible” (Hebrews 11:27).

Transient. Proskaira: for a season. Houses, careers, health, reputations, even suffering.

What it does not mean. Not that the physical world is unreal or unimportant. God made it good and will renew it (Romans 8:21). It means not making the passing things the focus of our hope.

On a Tuesday. Try ending each day by asking: what did I spend my attention on today? Then spend a few minutes looking at the unseen: read a promise of God about the life to come and give thanks.

5.title: The Heavenly Dwelling, the Judgment Seat, and the Ministry of Reconciliation
5.overview:
Paul has just said that his outer self is wasting away and that he looks to what is unseen. Now he explains why death does not frighten him. If this tent, our present body, is taken down, we have a building from God, eternal in the heavens. We groan now, longing not to be stripped bare but to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling, so that what is mortal is swallowed up by life; and God has given the Spirit as a down payment. So Paul is courageous: he would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord. Either way, his aim is to please him, because all must appear before the judgement seat of Christ.

That fear of the Lord, and above all the love of Christ, drives his ministry. One died for all, so all died, so that the living should live for him. Anyone in Christ is a new creation. God has reconciled us to himself through Christ, not counting our sins against us, and has made Paul an ambassador with a message: be reconciled to God. The chapter ends with one of the greatest sentences in Scripture: God made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Heavenly Dwelling and the Judgment Seat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul explains why death does not frighten him. The present body is like a tent that will one day be taken down, but God has a permanent dwelling ready. Believers long to receive it, not to be left without a body but to have mortality swallowed up by life, and the Spirit is God’s guarantee. So Paul is confident: to leave the body is to be at home with the Lord, which he would prefer. Either way, his ambition is to please Christ, because everyone will stand before Christ’s judgement seat and give account for their life in the body.
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment seat of Christ (v. 10) is a significant and sometimes neglected doctrine. Reformed theology insists on two distinct judgments: the justification that settles the believer’s eternal standing (entirely by grace, through faith, in Christ — Rom. 8:1: “no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus”) and the assessment of the believer’s life and works (1 Cor. 3:10–15; 2 Cor. 5:10; Rev. 22:12). At the bēma, salvation is not at stake; stewardship is. This distinction protects the gospel of grace while maintaining genuine accountability for the quality of the Christian life.
verseByVerse.examples: A Christian professional justifies a series of ethical compromises in his career with the thought that “grace covers everything.” He is not wrong about grace — but he is using it as a licence rather than a motivation. The judgment seat of Christ does not threaten his justification; it does call him to account for the quality of his stewardship. Paul says the knowledge of the judgment seat motivates him to “persuade others” (v. 11) — it is a motivating, not a threatening, reality for the justified believer.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we know that if the tent we live in on earth, our present body, is taken down, we have a building from God: a home not made by human hands, eternal, in heaven.

A tentmaker’s picture. Paul made tents for a living (Acts 18:3). A tent is temporary, flimsy, and is taken down when the journey moves on. Israel lived in tents in the wilderness; the tabernacle itself was a tent until the temple was built. Our present body is the tent; the resurrection body is the permanent building.

Not made with hands. A phrase for what God does directly (Mark 14:58; Hebrews 9:11). The resurrection body is God’s work.

We know. Not “we hope” or “we guess”. Certainty grounded in Christ’s resurrection (4:14).

What is the building? Most take it as the resurrection body. Some take it as heaven itself, or the church as Christ’s body. Verdict: the resurrection body, since it is contrasted with “our earthly tent” and is something we “put on” (vv. 2–4; compare 1 Corinthians 15:53).

On a Tuesday. At a funeral, when the coffin is lowered, remember that the tent has been taken down. The building is waiting.
verseByVerse.note: Paul, a tentmaker by trade, pictures the present body as a tent — temporary — and the resurrection body as a permanent building.

parallels.desc: houses of clay

verseByVerse.quote: For in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling, if indeed by putting it on we may not be found naked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meanwhile, in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly home over it, so that by putting it on we will not be found naked.

Groan. The groaning of creation and of believers waiting for “the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:22–23). Not complaint but longing.

Put on. Paul mixes his metaphors: a house you put on like clothing. Both point to the body.

Naked. Greeks often thought of the soul without the body as freed, like a bird out of a cage. For a Jew, being disembodied was like being naked: incomplete, exposed. Paul shrinks from the state of a soul without a body, even though, for a believer, it means being with Christ (v. 8).

A textual note. Most early manuscripts read “by putting it on” (endysamenoi). A few read “by taking it off” (ekdysamenoi), followed by some editors and the NRSV, which avoids what seems a repetition. The first is better attested and fits Paul’s point: once clothed with the new body, we will not be naked.

On a Tuesday. Christian hope is not to escape the body but to receive a new one. Look after your body now as a gift; long for the body to come.

verseByVerse.quote: For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened—not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For while we are in this tent, we groan under the burden. It is not that we want to be stripped of our body, but that we want to be clothed over with the new, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.

Burdened. By weakness, ageing and the prospect of death.

Further clothed. Ependysasthai: to put on over. Paul would prefer to be alive when Christ returns and be changed without dying (1 Corinthians 15:51–52), the new body put on over the old.

Swallowed up by life. Echoing Isaiah 25:8: “He will swallow up death forever.” “Death is swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54). Death does not swallow life; life swallows death.

On a Tuesday. If you fear the process of dying more than death itself, you are in good company: so did Paul. Bring that fear to God honestly.

verseByVerse.quote: He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is God who has prepared us for this very purpose, and he has given us the Spirit as a down payment of what is to come.

Prepared. Katergasamenos: shaped, made ready. God designed us for resurrection life. This is what we were made for.

The Spirit as guarantee. Arrabōn, as in 1:22: a deposit, the first instalment of the full payment. The life of the Spirit now is a foretaste of the resurrection life to come (Romans 8:11).

For worship. Thank God that every stirring of the Spirit in you, every answered prayer, every sense of his love, is a down payment on the resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “guarantee” was used for a deposit or first instalment, pledging full payment later.

verseByVerse.quote: So we are always of good courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord, for we walk by faith, not by sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we are always confident. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord, for we live by faith, not by sight.

Courage. Tharrountes: cheerful confidence, good courage. Despite groaning.

At home, away. Endēmeō, ekdēmeō: to live among your own people, to be abroad. In the body we are, in a sense, abroad from the Lord: not that he is absent (Matthew 28:20), but we do not see him face to face.

Faith, not sight. We trust what we cannot see (Hebrews 11:1). The Christian life is lived on God’s word, not on visible proof.

On a Tuesday. When God seems absent, that is what “walking by faith” feels like. Keep walking.

verseByVerse.quote: Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yes, we are confident, and we would much prefer to leave our home in the body and go to be at home with the Lord.

Away from the body. At death, before the resurrection, the believer is “at home with the Lord”. This is the intermediate state.

What happens at death? Christians hold several views.

Soul sleep: the dead are unconscious until the resurrection (Seventh-day Adventists; many conditionalists).

Purgatory: most believers are purified after death before entering heaven (Roman Catholic).

Immediate resurrection: some scholars think Paul here expects the new body at the moment of death.

Conscious presence with Christ: the soul is with the Lord in conscious joy while awaiting the resurrection of the body (the historic Protestant view, Westminster Confession 32.1).

Verdict: the last. “At home with the Lord” is not unconscious sleep. Jesus promised the thief, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Paul says departing to be with Christ is “far better” (Philippians 1:23), which would hardly be true of unconsciousness. Purgatory has no basis here: Paul expects to be with the Lord, not in a place of cleansing; Christ’s blood has cleansed (1 John 1:7). And the resurrection of the body remains a future event at Christ’s return (1 Thessalonians 4:16), so the intermediate state is real but incomplete.

On a Tuesday. When a Christian you love dies, they are not asleep in a box, nor in a fire. They are at home with the Lord. Grieve, but with hope.

verseByVerse.quote: So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So whether we are at home in the body or away from it, we make it our ambition to please him. For all of us must appear before the judgement seat of Christ, so that each of us may receive what we deserve for what we have done in the body, whether good or bad.

Our aim. Philotimoumetha: literally “we love the honour”, we make it our ambition. A word for public ambition, here redirected: Paul’s only ambition is to please Christ.

The judgement seat. Bēma: the raised platform from which a Roman magistrate gave judgement. In Corinth’s forum there was a large stone bēma, still visible today, and Paul had stood before the proconsul Gallio there (Acts 18:12–17). Every Corinthian could picture it. Romans 14:10 speaks of the judgement seat of God; here it is Christ’s, because the Father has given all judgement to the Son (John 5:22).

Will Christians be judged? Yes, but not to decide whether they are saved. “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Believers are judged for their works, which show the reality of their faith, and receive reward or loss. Some will be saved “only as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3:13–15).

Faith and works. Roman Catholic teaching says final justification includes the merit of good works done in grace. Verdict: the Reformed view (Westminster Confession 33.1): all will be judged according to their works, but believers are justified by Christ’s righteousness alone. Their works are the evidence, not the ground. God graciously rewards works he himself produced.

On a Tuesday. What you do in your body matters: how you spend your money, treat your spouse, do your job, use your phone. It will be seen by Christ. Not to terrify you, but to make your ordinary week weighty.
verseByVerse.note: The judgment seat (bema) was the raised platform where a Roman official gave judgment; Paul had stood before one in Corinth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — The Ministry of Reconciliation and the Great Exchange
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Knowing the fear of the Lord, Paul tries to persuade people, and he hopes the Corinthians can see his sincerity and answer those who boast in appearances. What drives him is Christ’s love: one died for all, so all who are his have died with him and now live for him. Paul no longer judges anyone, Christ included, by worldly standards; whoever is in Christ belongs to the new creation. God has reconciled people to himself through Christ, not counting their sins against them, and has made Paul his envoy, pleading with people to accept that reconciliation. The ground of it all is an exchange: the sinless Christ was treated as sin for us, so that in him we might be counted righteous before God.
verseByVerse.theology:
“In Christ God was reconciling the world to himself” (v. 19) — the agency is God’s. Reconciliation is initiated, accomplished, and offered by God, not by humanity. The word order matters and is often misquoted: it is not that God was waiting to be reconciled to humanity, as if he needed to be persuaded or appeased by a more merciful Son. Rather, God himself was the reconciler — the one who, in Christ, removed the obstacle that prevented humanity from being reconciled to him. The obstacle is sin; the removal is the cross, and v. 21 states its cost.

Verse 21 — “he made him to be sin who knew no sin” — requires precise handling. “Made him to be sin” does not mean Christ became a sinner or had sinful desires. It means God treated Christ as the sin-bearer — the one who stood in the place of sinners, receiving the judgment that sin deserves. The Old Testament background is the sin offering: in Leviticus the offering itself is called by the same word as the sin it carried, the animal becoming the sin-bearer, and Isaiah says it without a picture at all — “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isa. 53:6). The result: we “become the righteousness of God” — not merely receive a righteous verdict but are constituted righteous in him, which is why the standing cannot be damaged by a bad week.
verseByVerse.examples: An evangelism trainer teaches his church that the goal of evangelism is to persuade people to make a decision for Christ. This passage suggests a deeper framework: the goal is to implore people, on Christ’s behalf, to be reconciled to God — as ambassadors of a reconciliation that God himself has already accomplished and is already offering. The difference is not merely semantic: the ambassador does not create the peace; he announces and conveys the peace that the King has already made.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. But what we are is known to God, and I hope it is known also to your conscience. We are not commending ourselves to you again but giving you cause to boast about us, so that you may be able to answer those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we know what it is to fear the Lord, we try to persuade people. God sees us exactly as we are, and I hope that you also see it in your consciences. We are not commending ourselves to you again. We are giving you a reason to be proud of us, so that you can answer those who take pride in outward show rather than in what is in the heart.

The fear of the Lord. Not terror, but reverent awe of the Judge of verse 10. Knowing that every person will stand before Christ, Paul cannot keep silent.

Persuade. Peithomen: to reason, argue, appeal. Paul argued in synagogues and the marketplace (Acts 17:2–4, 17; 18:4). Persuasion is not manipulation (4:2); it is giving reasons.

Outward appearance. The rival teachers boasted of eloquence, visions and Jewish credentials (11:22; 12:1). God looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).

On a Tuesday. If you believe your colleagues will stand before Christ, it should change how you talk with them: gently, but with reasons for the hope that is in you (1 Peter 3:15).

verseByVerse.quote: For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we seem out of our minds, it is for God. If we are in our right minds, it is for you.

Beside ourselves. Exestēmen: out of one’s mind, ecstatic. Two readings:

Paul’s ecstatic spiritual experiences, visions or tongues (12:1–4; 1 Corinthians 14:18), which are between him and God, not for public display.

The charge that he is mad, a fanatic. Jesus’ family said, “He is out of his mind” (Mark 3:21). Festus told Paul, “Paul, you are out of your mind” (Acts 26:24).

Verdict: possibly both. Whatever people think of his zeal, it is for God; his sober teaching is for them. Either way, nothing is for himself.

On a Tuesday. If people think you are too religious, remember Paul and Jesus were thought mad. But make sure your public faith is sane, clear and for others’ good.

verseByVerse.quote: For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died; and he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the love of Christ leaves us no choice, because we are convinced of this: one man died for all, and therefore all died. And he died for all so that those who are alive should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and was raised.

The love of Christ. Christ’s love for us, not ours for him. “Controls” (synechei) means hems in, presses on, compels, like a river between banks. It is the engine of Paul’s life.

One died for all. Substitution: one in the place of many. “Therefore all died”: in his death, those for whom he died died with him. “Our old self was crucified with him” (Romans 6:6); “I have been crucified with Christ” (Galatians 2:20).

Who are the “all”?

Arminian and many other Christians read “all” as every human being: Christ died to make salvation possible for everyone, and it becomes effective for those who believe.

The Reformed view (definite atonement) reads “all” as all who are in Christ: those for whom he died are those who died with him and now live for him. Paul’s logic is that the “all” for whom he died are the same “all” who died with him, and that leads to new life.

Verdict: definite atonement best fits the passage. Not every human being has died to sin and been raised to new life. The death actually accomplishes something for those it was for. But this conviction should make us more, not less, eager to proclaim Christ to everyone (v. 20). Christians on both sides of this question have been great evangelists.

No longer for themselves. The purpose of the cross is a changed life. To live for yourself after Christ died for you is to contradict the meaning of his death.

On a Tuesday. Before deciding how to spend Saturday, your bonus or your retirement, ask: am I living for myself, or for him who died for me?

verseByVerse.quote: From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So from now on we do not regard anyone from a merely human point of view. Even though we once thought of Christ in that way, we no longer do so. So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation. The old has gone; look, the new has come!

According to the flesh. By worldly standards: status, race, wealth, eloquence. The Corinthians judged Paul that way. Paul once judged Jesus that way.

Did Paul know Jesus personally? Some have taken “we once regarded Christ according to the flesh” to mean Paul had met Jesus before the crucifixion, or that Paul is dismissing interest in the historical Jesus. Verdict: neither. Paul means that he once evaluated Jesus by worldly standards: a crucified failure, cursed by God (Galatians 3:13). Now he knows him as Lord. Paul cares deeply about the historical facts of Jesus’ life, death and resurrection (1 Corinthians 11:23–26; 15:3–8).

A new creation. The Greek has no verb: “if anyone in Christ, new creation!” Two senses, both true:

Personal: the believer is a new person.

Cosmic: by being in Christ, the believer belongs already to the new creation God promised: “For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17); “Behold, I am doing a new thing” (Isaiah 43:19). It has begun in Christ’s resurrection and will be completed when he says, “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5).

A textual note. Later manuscripts (KJV “all things are become new”) add “all things”. The earliest read simply “the new has come”. The addition is a natural expansion.

On a Tuesday. When you meet a new Christian with a bad past, an ex-prisoner or a recovering addict, do not see them by the old record. If they are in Christ, they are a new creation. And neither should you see yourself by your old record.

parallels.desc: behold, I am doing a new thing

verseByVerse.quote: All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation; that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All of this comes from God. Through Christ he reconciled us to himself, and he gave us the ministry of reconciliation. That is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting people’s sins against them, and he has entrusted us with the message of reconciliation.

From God. The initiative is entirely God’s. We were the offenders; he made the peace.

Reconcile. Katallassō: to change enmity into friendship. In Greek it was used of estranged husbands and wives, or nations making peace. Here the estrangement is between sinners and a holy God. The barrier is not only our hostility to God but his just wrath against sin (Romans 5:9–10). Christ removes both.

In Christ God was reconciling. Two possible readings: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world” (KJV, pointing to the incarnation) or “in Christ God was reconciling the world” (ESV, pointing to the cross). Verdict: the second fits the sentence best, though both are true.

The world. Does this mean every person is already reconciled? Universalists say so. Verdict: no. The next verse urges people to “be reconciled to God”, which makes no sense if they already are. “The world” means God’s reconciling work is for people of every nation, not only Israel; it is received by faith (Romans 5:11).

Not counting their trespasses. Accounting language. “Blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin” (Romans 4:8, quoting Psalm 32:2). Sins are not counted against us because they were counted against Christ (v. 21).

On a Tuesday. If you are reconciled to God, you have a message to share and a model to follow. Is there a broken relationship you could take the first step to mend?

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we are ambassadors for Christ; God is making his appeal through us. We plead with you on Christ’s behalf: be reconciled to God.

Ambassadors. Presbeuomen. In the Roman world an envoy (presbeutēs, in Latin legatus) represented the emperor in a province and spoke with his authority. The ambassador does not make up his message; he delivers the king’s.

God making his appeal. When the gospel is preached faithfully, God himself speaks. The Second Helvetic Confession says, “The preaching of the Word of God is the Word of God.”

Implore. Deometha: beg, plead. The king’s envoy pleading with rebels to accept terms of peace. Amazing condescension.

Be reconciled. Passive: allow yourselves to be reconciled, accept what God has done. Paul says it even to the Corinthian church, because some were drifting from the gospel.

On a Tuesday. Every Christian is an ambassador. When you speak to your neighbour about Christ, you speak for the King. Speak with his authority and with his pleading heart.
verseByVerse.note: An ambassador spoke with the authority of the king who sent him.

verseByVerse.quote: For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For our sake God made him who never knew sin to be sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

Who knew no sin. Jesus never sinned (Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22). “Knew” means had no personal experience of it.

Made him to be sin. Not that Christ became sinful. Two explanations:

Sin offering: in the Greek Old Testament the word “sin” (hamartia) is sometimes used for the sin offering (Leviticus 4:24; Isaiah 53:10, “an offering for guilt”). Augustine read it this way.

Treated as a sinner: God laid our sins on him and treated him as sin deserves. “The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6).

Verdict: the two belong together. Christ became the sin offering by having our sin imputed to him and bearing its penalty.

The great exchange. Our sin is counted to him; his righteousness is counted to us. Luther called it the “wonderful exchange”. “The righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18). God remains “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).

Become the righteousness of God. N. T. Wright and others argue that this means Paul and his fellow apostles embody God’s covenant faithfulness in their ministry. Verdict: the parallel with the first half decides it. Christ was made sin, not by becoming sinful, but by imputation; so we become righteousness, not by becoming sinless, but by imputation. This is the heart of justification. “The LORD is our righteousness” (Jeremiah 23:6).

On a Tuesday. When your conscience accuses you, answer it with this verse. Your sins were counted to Christ. His righteousness is counted to you. The account is settled.

For worship. Hymn: “Bearing shame and scoffing rude, in my place condemned he stood; sealed my pardon with his blood: Hallelujah! What a Saviour!” (Philip Bliss).

parallels.desc: he was pierced for our transgressions

6.title: The Open Heart, the Catalogue of Hardships, and the Unequal Yoke
6.overview:
Having said that God makes his appeal through his ambassadors, Paul makes it: do not receive God’s grace in vain, for now is the day of salvation. Then he shows the Corinthians what a true servant of God looks like, in one of the most powerful passages he ever wrote. It is not a list of successes but of endurance: beatings, prisons, riots, sleepless nights and hunger, and alongside them purity, kindness, the Holy Spirit and genuine love. He lives in paradoxes: treated as an impostor yet true, dying yet alive, sorrowful yet always rejoicing, poor yet making many rich, having nothing yet possessing everything. He has opened his heart wide to them; he asks them to open theirs.

Then a sudden, sharp section (6:14–7:1): do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. Light has nothing in common with darkness, nor Christ with Belial, nor God’s temple with idols. The church is the temple of the living God, as the prophets promised, so it must come out and be separate from idolatry and impurity, and God will be a Father to his sons and daughters.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Open Heart and the Catalogue of Hardships
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As God’s fellow workers, Paul urges the Corinthians not to let God’s grace come to nothing in them: the time of God’s favour that Isaiah promised has arrived. He takes care that his conduct puts no obstacle in anyone’s way. His credentials are not successes but endurance in hardship, beatings, prison, riots, overwork and hunger, together with purity, patience, kindness, the Spirit, love and truthful speech. His life is full of paradox: dishonoured yet honoured, called a fraud yet genuine, dying yet alive, grieving yet always glad, poor yet enriching many, owning nothing yet possessing everything. He has opened his heart to them and asks them to open theirs in return.
verseByVerse.theology: The catalogue of hardships (vv. 4–5) is one of several in 2 Corinthians (cf. 4:8–9; 11:23–29; 12:10). Together they constitute Paul’s theology of the cross applied to ministry: the authentic apostle is identified not by spectacular results or impressive presence but by the pattern of cruciform suffering. This does not glorify suffering for its own sake; it identifies the shape that kingdom advance takes in a world that crucified its King. Those who carry the message of the cross will bear in their bodies the pattern of the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: A young minister enters a hard urban church plant with ambitions of rapid growth and visible impact. After three years, he has a small congregation, many failures, and a life that looks more like Paul’s catalogue than his vision board. He questions his calling. This passage is the specific word for him: the catalogue of hardships is not evidence of failed ministry but of authentic ministry. The question is not whether ministry is fruitful by visible metrics but whether the minister is conducting himself with the character described in vv. 6–7.

verseByVerse.quote: Working together with him, then, we appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says, “In a favorable time I listened to you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you.” Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As people working together with God, we urge you not to receive God’s grace and let it come to nothing. For he says, “At the time of my favour I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” Look, now is the time of favour; now is the day of salvation.

Working together. With God (5:20), as his ambassadors. Paul is God’s fellow worker (1 Corinthians 3:9), not his equal.

In vain. Eis kenon: to no purpose, empty. Does this mean a true Christian can lose salvation? Arminian readers say it warns of that possibility. Verdict: Paul is warning a church where some were being drawn to a different gospel (11:4). A person can hear the gospel, profess it and yet show that they never truly received it (1 Corinthians 15:2, “unless you believed in vain”). For true believers, the warning is one of the means by which God keeps them. Paul could say of himself, “his grace toward me was not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Isaiah 49:8. In Isaiah, God speaks to his Servant, promising to help him restore Israel and bring salvation to the nations. Paul sees that promise fulfilled in Christ. The age of God’s favour has begun, as Jesus announced in Nazareth, “to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor” (Luke 4:19).

Now. Not tomorrow. “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15).

On a Tuesday. If you have been meaning to get right with God, to forgive someone, or to come back to church, today is the day. Do not wait for a better time.

parallels.desc: in a time of favour I have answered you

verseByVerse.quote: We put no obstacle in anyone’s way, so that no fault may be found with our ministry,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are careful to put no stumbling block in anyone’s way, so that no one can find fault with our ministry.

No obstacle. Paul refused payment at Corinth (11:7–9) and gave up his rights (1 Corinthians 9:12) so that no one could say he preached for money. The offence should be the cross itself (Galatians 5:11), not the preacher’s behaviour.

On a Tuesday. A Christian manager who is harsh, or a Christian plumber who overcharges, puts a stumbling block before the gospel. Make sure people stumble over Christ, not over you.

verseByVerse.quote: but as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: by great endurance, in afflictions, hardships, calamities, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, sleepless nights, hunger;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead, as God’s servants, we show what we are in every way: by great endurance in troubles, hardships and distresses, in beatings, imprisonments and riots, in hard work, sleepless nights and hunger.

A new kind of reference. The rival teachers commended themselves by success. Paul commends himself by what he has endured. In the ancient world, philosophers sometimes listed hardships to show their virtue; Paul does it to show God’s power in weakness.

Endurance first. Hypomonē, the quality that holds the rest together.

Three groups of three.

General troubles: afflictions, hardships, calamities (narrow places with no way out).

Inflicted by others: beatings (at Philippi, Acts 16:23), imprisonments, riots (Ephesus, Acts 19).

Self-chosen for the gospel: labours, sleepless nights, going without food (fasting or simply hunger).

On a Tuesday. Faithfulness under pressure is a better reference than any success. The missionary who stayed twenty years with little fruit, the wife who stayed with a difficult husband, the employee who would not lie for the boss: these commend themselves as servants of God.

verseByVerse.quote: by purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love; by truthful speech, and the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left;
verseByVerse.commentary:
We show it by purity, knowledge, patience and kindness; by the Holy Spirit and sincere love; by truthful speech and the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness in the right hand and in the left.

The inner qualities. After the hardships, the character. Purity (moral integrity), knowledge (of God and the gospel), patience (makrothymia, long-temperedness with people), kindness. These are fruits of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22).

The Holy Spirit. In the middle of the list, the source of all of it.

Right hand and left. A soldier carried his sword or spear in the right hand and his shield in the left. Righteousness equips Paul for attack and defence (Ephesians 6:14–17). Some think it means righteousness in both good times and bad, which leads into verse 8.

On a Tuesday. Patience and kindness with a slow colleague or a difficult relative are as much a mark of ministry as preaching. Ask the Spirit for them.
verseByVerse.note: Weapons “for the right hand and for the left” are weapons for attack (the sword) and defence (the shield).

verseByVerse.quote: through honor and dishonor, through slander and praise. We are treated as impostors, and yet are true; as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as punished, and yet not killed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
We serve through honour and dishonour, through bad reports and good. We are treated as frauds, yet we are genuine; as unknown, yet we are well known; as dying, yet look, we are alive; as punished, yet not killed.

Paradoxes. Paul’s life looks one way to the world and is another way before God.

Impostors. The rival teachers called Paul a deceiver (12:16). The Jewish leaders called Jesus a deceiver (Matthew 27:63). Paul shares his Lord’s reputation.

Unknown, well known. Insignificant to Rome’s elite, but known to God and to the churches.

Dying, we live. Echoing Psalm 118:17–18: “I shall not die, but I shall live … The LORD has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death.”

On a Tuesday. When you are misunderstood at work or misrepresented online for following Christ, remember: what matters is how God sees you.

verseByVerse.quote: as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; poor, yet making many rich; having nothing, yet possessing everything.

Sorrowful, rejoicing. Not alternating moods, but both at once. Paul weeps over sin and suffering and rejoices in the Lord.

Poor, making many rich. Like Christ, “who though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (8:9). Paul worked with his hands and often went hungry, but he brought eternal riches to thousands.

Having nothing, possessing everything. “All things are yours … and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s” (1 Corinthians 3:21–23). The meek “shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5).

On a Tuesday. A pensioner on a small income who gives generously and prays faithfully is rich. A businessman with everything who has no Christ has nothing. Which are you, really?

For worship. Thank God that in Christ you possess everything, whatever your bank balance says.

verseByVerse.quote: We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians; our heart is wide open. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have spoken openly to you, Corinthians. Our heart is wide open to you. We are not holding back our affection for you; it is you who are holding back yours.

Corinthians! Paul rarely addresses a church by name in the middle of a letter (compare Galatians 3:1; Philippians 4:15). It is emotional, direct.

Our heart is wide open. A Hebrew picture: a wide heart is a loving, generous heart (Psalm 119:32). Paul hides nothing.

Restricted. Stenochōreisthe: cramped, squeezed. Their affections are narrow, not his. The problem in the relationship is on their side.

On a Tuesday. In a strained relationship, ask honestly: is the narrowness in me? Open your heart first.

verseByVerse.quote: In return (I speak as to children) widen your hearts also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In return, and I am speaking to you as my children, open your hearts wide to us too.

As to children. Paul is their spiritual father (1 Corinthians 4:14–15). A father pleads with his children for love.

Widen your hearts. Make room for us. The plea is repeated in 7:2.

On a Tuesday. Parents of grown-up children who have drifted away can pray this verse. Keep your heart wide open, and wait.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–7:1 — Do Not Be Unequally Yoked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul warns them not to bind themselves in partnerships with unbelievers that compromise their loyalty to Christ. Righteousness and lawlessness, light and darkness, Christ and Satan, God’s temple and idols have nothing in common. The church is God’s temple, the place where he has promised to live among his people. So, drawing on several prophetic promises, Paul calls them to leave idolatry and impurity behind, and God will welcome them as his sons and daughters. Holding such promises, they should cleanse themselves from everything that defiles body and spirit and pursue holiness in reverence for God.
verseByVerse.theology: The passage has been applied to several specific situations: (1) Marriage between believers and unbelievers — the most common application, supported by the principle if not the primary context. 1 Cor. 7:39 (she is free to marry “only in the Lord”) is the direct marriage prohibition. (2) Formal religious partnerships — interfaith worship, ecumenical agreements that require treating fundamental doctrinal differences as unimportant. (3) Business partnerships that require ethical compromise. The principle is: any relationship of primary spiritual allegiance that requires pulling in the same direction as one who is opposed to Christ creates an incompatible yoke. Ordinary friendship, working relationships, and engagement with unbelievers are not in view — Paul explicitly says in 1 Cor. 5:9–10 that he did not mean to avoid all contact with the immoral of the world.
verseByVerse.examples: A senior pastor receives an invitation to co-host a community prayer service with leaders from several faiths, including those who explicitly deny the Trinity and the uniqueness of Christ as Saviour. He must decide whether this is a civic engagement (speaking to the community) or a spiritual partnership (worshipping together). This passage suggests the distinction matters: representing the church’s concern for the community is different from implying that all faith traditions are pulling the same spiritual yoke toward the same God.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be harnessed together with unbelievers in a mismatched yoke. For what do righteousness and lawlessness have in common? What fellowship can light have with darkness?

The picture. “You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together” (Deuteronomy 22:10). Two animals of different kinds, size and strength cannot pull the same plough; they will pull against each other. “Unequally yoked” (heterozygountes) is literally “differently yoked”.

What did it mean in Corinth? In context, probably joining in pagan temple meals and idolatrous associations (v. 16; compare 1 Corinthians 8–10), and perhaps following the false apostles. Corinth had temples to Aphrodite, Apollo, Asclepius and the emperor; trade guilds and social life often met in them.

How far does it apply?

Marriage: almost all Christians apply it to marrying an unbeliever. Paul elsewhere says a widow may marry “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39). This is a clear and right application. It does not tell those already married to an unbeliever to leave (1 Corinthians 7:12–14).

Business: some apply it to all partnerships with unbelievers; others only to partnerships where the Christian’s obedience would be controlled or compromised. (See the study on Christians in business.)

Religious alliances: joint worship or ministry with those who deny the gospel.

Verdict: the principle is any binding partnership that would pull a Christian away from Christ or into idolatry. Marriage is the clearest case. Ordinary friendship, work and neighbourliness with unbelievers are not forbidden; to avoid all contact “you would need to go out of the world” (1 Corinthians 5:10). Jesus prayed not that we be taken out of the world, but kept from the evil one (John 17:15).

Does this section belong here? Because 6:14–7:1 seems to interrupt the appeal of 6:13 and 7:2, and uses some unusual words, some scholars think it is a fragment added later, perhaps from another letter. Verdict: no manuscript lacks it, and the flow makes sense. Paul asks them to open their hearts to him and close them to the idols and false teachers who are drawing them away.

On a Tuesday. If you are a single Christian falling for someone who does not share your faith, this verse is for you. It is hard, and it is kind. Talk to a trusted Christian friend before your heart is fully given.
verseByVerse.note: The picture comes from the law forbidding an ox and a donkey to be yoked together at the plough.

verseByVerse.quote: What accord has Christ with Belial? Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What harmony is there between Christ and Belial? What does a believer share with an unbeliever?

Belial. From a Hebrew word meaning “worthlessness” (beliyya‘al), used in the Old Testament for wicked people (“worthless men”, Deuteronomy 13:13; 1 Samuel 2:12). In Jewish writings of Paul’s time, including the Dead Sea Scrolls, Belial became a name for Satan, the leader of the forces of darkness. This is its only appearance in the New Testament.

Accord. Symphōnēsis, from which we get “symphony”: harmony. Christ and Satan cannot play in the same orchestra.

A believer and an unbeliever. Not that they cannot be friends or neighbours, but that in the deepest things, allegiance and worship, they belong to different kingdoms.

On a Tuesday. Love your unbelieving friends deeply. But do not pretend that you share the same ultimate loyalty. Honesty about the difference is part of love.
verseByVerse.note: Belial (“worthlessness”) was a Jewish name for Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, “I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What agreement can God’s temple have with idols? For we are the temple of the living God. As God said: “I will live among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people.”

Temple and idols. In the Old Testament, the worst sacrilege was putting an idol in God’s temple. King Manasseh did it (2 Kings 21:7); Antiochus IV did it (Daniel 11:31). The church is now the temple, so idolatry within it is sacrilege.

We are the temple. The church corporately (1 Corinthians 3:16–17) and each believer’s body (1 Corinthians 6:19).

The promise. A combination of Leviticus 26:11–12 (“I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people”) and Ezekiel 37:27 (God’s dwelling with his restored people in the new covenant). The covenant formula “I will be their God and they shall be my people” runs through the whole Bible to Revelation 21:3.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (KJV “ye are the temple”) read “you are”. The earliest read “we are”, including Paul with them. Both are true.

On a Tuesday. An idol is whatever you trust, love or fear more than God: money, career, a relationship, a political cause. Is there an idol in the temple?

parallels.desc: I will walk among you and be your God

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore go out from their midst, and be separate from them, says the Lord, and touch no unclean thing; then I will welcome you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, “Come out from among them and be separate,” says the Lord, “and touch nothing unclean; then I will welcome you.”

Isaiah 52:11. “Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing.” Originally a call to the exiles to leave Babylon and its idols and return home, carrying the temple vessels. Paul applies it to the church in Corinth.

I will welcome you. Probably from Ezekiel 20:34 (Greek): God gathering his people from the nations.

What it does not mean. Not physical withdrawal from society into a Christian enclave, but separation from idolatry and sin. The monastic movement and some separatist groups have taken it as a call to leave the world. Paul’s concern is moral and spiritual separation, not geographic.

On a Tuesday. Is there a group, habit or entertainment you need to leave because it keeps drawing you into sin? Leaving may cost friends. God promises to welcome you.

parallels.desc: depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing

verseByVerse.quote: and I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And I will be a Father to you, and you will be my sons and daughters,” says the Lord Almighty.

2 Samuel 7:14. God’s promise to David about his son: “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son.” Fulfilled first in Christ, the Son of David (Hebrews 1:5). Now extended to all who are in him.

Sons and daughters. Paul adds “daughters”, probably from Isaiah 43:6: “bring my sons from afar and my daughters from the end of the earth.” Women are as fully God’s children and heirs as men (Galatians 3:26–29).

The Lord Almighty. Pantokratōr, the Greek for “LORD of hosts”: the ruler of all. The almighty God as a Father.

On a Tuesday. Separation from the world is not loss but adoption. You leave idols and gain a Father.

For worship. Pray “Our Father” today, slowly, aware that the Almighty has made you his son or daughter.

parallels.desc: I will be to him a father
bring my sons and my daughters
