7.title: Godly Grief and the Joy of Reconciliation
7.overview:
Chapter 7 finishes two things. First, the call to holiness: since God has promised to live among his people and be their Father, they must cleanse themselves from everything that defiles body and spirit (7:1). Second, the story Paul broke off at 2:13. He had left Troas in anxiety and gone into Macedonia, where he found no rest: fighting outside, fear inside. Then Titus arrived with news from Corinth. The severe letter had hurt them, but the hurt had led to repentance. They had grieved, longed for Paul, and dealt with the offender.

So Paul explains the difference between two kinds of sorrow. Godly grief produces repentance that leads to salvation and leaves no regret; worldly grief produces death. He lists what their godly grief produced: earnestness, eagerness to clear themselves, indignation, fear, longing, zeal and readiness to see justice done. Titus has been refreshed by them, Paul’s boasting about them has proved true, and he rejoices that he can have complete confidence in them.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we have these promises, dear friends, let us wash ourselves clean of everything that pollutes body and spirit, and bring our holiness to completion out of reverence for God.

These promises. The ones just quoted (6:16–18): God dwelling among us, welcoming us, being our Father. Holiness is not the price of these promises but the response to them.

Body and spirit. Defilement of the body: sexual sin, drunkenness, temple prostitution (common in Corinth; 1 Corinthians 6:15–20). Defilement of the spirit: idolatry, pride, bitterness, false doctrine. Both matter; the whole person belongs to God.

Let us cleanse ourselves. God cleanses us in Christ (1 John 1:7), and we are called to cleanse ourselves. Not contradiction, but the pattern of Philippians 2:12–13: we work out what God works in.

Bringing holiness to completion. Epitelountes: carrying through to the end. Not that we achieve perfection in this life (Philippians 3:12), but that we press on towards it. “Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord” (Hebrews 12:14).

In the fear of God. Reverence for the holy Father, not terror of a tyrant.

On a Tuesday. Name one thing that is defiling you, body or spirit: a website, a habit, a grudge. Get rid of it this week, not to earn God’s love, but because he is your Father.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 2–16 — Godly Grief, Worldly Grief, and Joy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks again for a place in their hearts, insisting he has wronged and exploited no one, and assuring them he says this in love, not accusation. He takes up the story from chapter 2: in Macedonia he had no rest, with conflict outside and fear inside, until God comforted him through Titus’s arrival and his news. The Corinthians had been grieved by the severe letter, and Paul briefly regretted sending it, but their grief led to repentance. He contrasts sorrow that turns to God and leads to salvation with worldly sorrow that leads to death, and lists the earnest, practical fruits their repentance produced. Titus was refreshed by them, Paul’s confidence in them proved justified, and he rejoices.
verseByVerse.theology: The distinction between godly grief and worldly grief is pastorally crucial. Worldly grief can look like repentance: tears, distress, self-accusation. But its focus is on the pain caused to oneself (loss of reputation, loss of relationships, loss of comfort) rather than on the offence against God. Judas displays worldly grief — he is distraught over what he has done, even returns the money, but cannot receive forgiveness; he destroys himself. Peter displays godly grief — the same tears, the same self-accusation, but directed toward the face of Jesus, resolved by Jesus’s restoration. The direction of the grief determines its outcome.
verseByVerse.examples: A pastor is confronted with evidence of long-term financial dishonesty. He weeps, expresses remorse, describes how devastated he is — by the damage to his reputation, the pain to his family, the end of his ministry. He never directly addresses the harm done to those he stole from, or the offence against God. His leadership team recognises, with the categories of this passage, that they are witnessing worldly grief — real grief, but pointed in the wrong direction. Genuine repentance would ask different questions: not “what have I lost?” but “against whom have I sinned, and what must I do to make it right?”

verseByVerse.quote: Make room in your hearts for us. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one. I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make room for us in your hearts. We have wronged no one, ruined no one, exploited no one. I am not saying this to condemn you. As I said before, you have such a place in our hearts that we would die with you or live with you.

Make room. Picking up 6:13: “widen your hearts also”. After the warning about false partnerships (6:14–7:1), Paul returns to the true one.

Three denials. Probably answering accusations. “Wronged” (injustice), “corrupted” (morally or doctrinally ruined), “taken advantage of” (pleonekteō, exploited for gain, perhaps over the collection for Jerusalem; compare 12:17–18). Paul’s conscience is clear.

Not to condemn. Paul quickly reassures. He is defending himself, not attacking them.

To die together and to live together. A phrase of lifelong friendship and loyalty in Greek writing: friends who would share life and death. Notice the order: die first, then live. In Christ, even death leads to life together.

On a Tuesday. When you have to defend yourself against an unfair accusation, do it without counter-attacking. Say what is true, then reaffirm your love.

verseByVerse.quote: I am acting with great boldness toward you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort. In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I speak to you with great openness; I am very proud of you. I am filled with encouragement. In all our troubles my joy overflows.

Boldness and pride. Parrēsia (frankness) and kauchēsis (boasting). Paul can speak openly and boast of them because the relationship is mended.

Overflowing with joy in affliction. Not after it, in it. The theme of the letter: comfort in affliction (1:3–7).

On a Tuesday. Tell someone in your church or family what you are proud of in them. Paul does, extravagantly.

verseByVerse.quote: For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn—fighting without and fear within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even after we arrived in Macedonia, our bodies had no rest. We were troubled on every side: quarrels outside, fears inside. But God, who comforts the downhearted, comforted us by the arrival of Titus.

The story resumes. From 2:12–13. Paul had left Troas and crossed to Macedonia, probably to Philippi or Thessalonica, hoping to meet Titus coming from Corinth.

Fighting without. Conflicts with opponents, perhaps persecution of the Macedonian churches (8:1–2).

Fear within. Anxiety for Corinth and for Titus, who was carrying money and had to travel dangerous roads. The great apostle was afraid. That is honest.

God who comforts the downcast. Echoing Isaiah 49:13: “the LORD has comforted his people and will have compassion on his afflicted.” “Downcast” (tapeinous) is the lowly, the humbled.

By the coming of Titus. God’s comfort came in the form of a friend at the door. God usually comforts through people.

On a Tuesday. You may be God’s answer to someone’s fear this week. A visit, a phone call or a message saying “I am here” can be the coming of Titus.
verseByVerse.note: Paul picks up the story he broke off in 2:13: waiting anxiously for Titus.

verseByVerse.quote: and not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And not only by his arrival, but also by the comfort you had given him. He told us how you long for me, how sorry you are, how eager you are to stand by me, so that I was even happier.

Comfort passed on. The Corinthians comforted Titus; Titus comforted Paul. Comfort travels (1:4).

Three reports. Longing (to see Paul again), mourning (sorrow for what had happened), zeal (for Paul, now defending him). Exactly the reverse of the painful visit.

On a Tuesday. Good news is worth delivering. “Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country” (Proverbs 25:25). If you hear something encouraging about someone, tell the person who will be most glad to hear it.

verseByVerse.quote: For even if I made you grieve with my letter, I do not regret it—though I did regret it, for I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even if my letter hurt you, I do not regret it. I did regret it for a while, because I see that it hurt you, though only briefly.

The tearful letter. See 2:3–4. Paul had agonised over sending it.

I did regret it. After sending it, Paul worried that it was too harsh, that it might drive them away. Every parent and pastor who has written a hard letter knows this feeling.

What it does not mean. Not that Paul thought the letter was wrong. His regret was the anxiety of love waiting for a response, not a confession of error. Feelings of regret are not always a sign that we did wrong.

Only for a while. The pain was temporary; the fruit was lasting.

On a Tuesday. After you have said something hard but necessary to a friend, you may lie awake regretting it. Wait for the fruit. Pray, and do not rush to take it back.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. For you felt a godly grief, so that you suffered no loss through us. For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I am glad, not because you were hurt, but because the hurt led you to repent. Your sorrow was the kind God wants, so you were not harmed in any way by us. For sorrow that comes from God produces a repentance that leads to salvation, which no one regrets; but the sorrow of the world produces death.

Two kinds of grief. This is one of the most practical distinctions in the Bible.

Godly grief (literally “grief according to God”) is sorrow over sin as an offence against God. It turns towards him, confesses, and changes.

Worldly grief is sorrow over consequences: being caught, losing face, suffering loss. It turns inward, to self-pity, shame, bitterness or despair, and leads to death.

Two examples. Peter and Judas both betrayed Jesus on the same night. Peter “went out and wept bitterly” (Matthew 26:75), and was restored. Judas “changed his mind” and returned the money (Matthew 27:3), then went and hanged himself. Esau sought the blessing “with tears” but “found no chance to repent” (Hebrews 12:17): he regretted the loss, not the sin. David’s psalm of confession shows the godly kind: “a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm 51:17).

Repentance as a gift. Repentance is not a work by which we earn forgiveness. “God has granted repentance that leads to life” (Acts 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25). Medieval theology distinguished contrition (sorrow from love of God) from attrition (sorrow from fear of punishment), and taught that attrition was enough with the sacrament of penance. The Reformers rejected the penitential system: repentance is a turning of the whole heart to God, wrought by the Spirit, and forgiveness rests on Christ alone (Westminster Confession 15).

Without regret. Either the repentance is never regretted, or the salvation is. Both are true. No one in heaven regrets having repented.

On a Tuesday. When you are sorry for something you did, ask: am I sorry because I wronged God and others, or because I was found out or because it cost me? If it is the second, take it to God until it becomes the first.

parallels.desc: Peter’s tears and Judas’s remorse

verseByVerse.quote: For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, but also what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment! At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look what this godly sorrow has produced in you: what seriousness, what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what alarm, what longing, what zeal, what readiness to see justice done! In every way you have shown yourselves innocent in this matter.

Seven fruits of true repentance.

Earnestness: taking the matter seriously instead of shrugging.

Eagerness to clear yourselves (apologia): putting things right, showing they did not approve of the wrong.

Indignation: anger at the sin and at themselves.

Fear: of God, or of Paul’s coming with discipline.

Longing: for Paul, for restored fellowship.

Zeal: energetic concern.

Punishment (ekdikēsis): justice done, the offender disciplined (2:6).

Innocent. Not that they had never sinned, but that by their response they had cleared themselves of complicity.

On a Tuesday. Real repentance shows itself. If you have wronged someone, it will look like seriousness, making amends, hatred of the sin and a desire to restore the relationship. Not just “sorry if you were offended.”

verseByVerse.quote: So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So although I wrote to you, it was not mainly because of the man who did wrong, nor because of the one who was wronged, but so that before God you could see for yourselves how devoted to us you really are.

The one who suffered the wrong. Probably Paul himself, speaking indirectly. Some think it was another person, perhaps a church member insulted on Paul’s behalf. Verdict: most likely Paul, who speaks of himself modestly.

The real purpose. The letter was not mainly about settling a quarrel. It was about the church discovering its own loyalty to the gospel and to the apostle God had sent. Sometimes a crisis shows a church what it really believes.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (KJV “our care for you”) reverse the pronouns. The earliest read “your earnestness for us”, which fits the context.

On a Tuesday. A church conflict handled well can leave a church stronger than before. Pray for that outcome in any dispute you are part of.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore we are comforted. And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all. For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is why we are encouraged. And on top of our own encouragement, we were especially delighted by how happy Titus was, because all of you set his mind at rest. I had boasted to him about you, and you did not let me down. Just as everything we told you was true, so our boasting to Titus about you has proved true as well.

Titus. A Gentile convert (Galatians 2:3), one of Paul’s most trusted co-workers. He had gone to Corinth with a difficult letter, probably nervous. He came back refreshed.

Paul’s boasting. Before sending Titus, Paul had told him the Corinthians would respond well. He took a risk on them. They proved him right.

True. Paul’s words to them and about them are both true. This answers the charge of fickleness (1:17–18).

On a Tuesday. Speak well of people to others before they have proved it. Sometimes your confidence helps them live up to it.

verseByVerse.quote: And his affection for you is even greater, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And his affection for you grows even more as he remembers how all of you obeyed, how you welcomed him with fear and trembling. I am glad that I can have complete confidence in you.

Fear and trembling. Not terror of Titus, but humble seriousness, knowing that he came as Paul’s representative and that the matter was before God (Philippians 2:12).

Complete confidence. Tharrō en panti: I am of good courage about you in everything. This prepares for chapters 8–9, where Paul will ask them to complete the collection for Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. If you are reconciled with someone, say so clearly: “I trust you.” Restored trust, spoken aloud, heals.

For worship. Thank God for broken relationships he has healed, in your church, family or life. Repentance and reconciliation are his work.

8.title: The Grace of Giving: Christ Became Poor
8.overview:
Chapters 8 and 9 are about money: the collection Paul was gathering from his Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. Some background helps. The Jerusalem church had been poor for years. There was a famine under the emperor Claudius (Acts 11:28–30), many believers had lost work or family support for following Jesus, and the church had many widows (Acts 6:1). When Paul’s apostleship was recognised in Jerusalem, the leaders asked him to “remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do” (Galatians 2:10). For Paul the collection was more than relief. It was a sign that Jews and Gentiles were one body: the Gentiles, who had shared in Israel’s spiritual blessings, were sharing material blessings in return (Romans 15:25–27). Corinth had started eagerly a year earlier (1 Corinthians 16:1–4), but the quarrel with Paul had stalled it.

In chapter 8 Paul encourages them to finish. He points to the poor, persecuted churches of Macedonia, who gave beyond their means and begged to take part, because they first gave themselves to the Lord. Above all he points to Christ, who though he was rich became poor for our sake, so that we might become rich. Giving should be willing, proportionate to what one has, and aimed at fairness between churches. Then Paul introduces the team who will collect the money, Titus and two trusted brothers, chosen so that the handling of the gift will be above suspicion before God and people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Macedonian Example and Christ Who Became Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He describes the Macedonian churches, who in severe trials and deep poverty gave joyfully and beyond their means, even begging to be allowed to take part, because they had first given themselves to the Lord. He urges the Corinthians, who excel in so much, to excel in this generosity too. It is not a command; it is a test of genuine love, measured against the example of Christ, who was rich yet became poor for their sake so that they might become rich. They began a year ago; now they should finish, giving in proportion to what they have. The aim is not to burden them but fairness between churches, as with the manna in the wilderness, where no one had too much or too little.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 9 is one of the key NT texts for the kenosis of the incarnation (alongside Phil. 2:5–8 and John 1:1–14). “Though he was rich” describes the pre-incarnate state of the Son — possessing all the resources of divine glory, honour, and power. “He became poor” describes the incarnation and more specifically the cross: the Son laid aside the exercise of divine prerogatives and took on the condition of creaturely poverty, ultimately the poverty of crucifixion and cursed death. “That you by his poverty might become rich” — the result is the enrichment of believers: forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, the inheritance of the new creation.
verseByVerse.examples: A church board is considering its annual budget and the portion allocated to mission outside its own walls. One member argues that they should ensure their own facilities and staff are well-funded before giving generously abroad. This passage holds before him the Macedonian model: churches in deep poverty begging to give. And the Christological ground: the Son of God did not ensure his own comfort before giving to others. The board’s question is not merely financial but spiritual: does this budget reflect the grace described in v. 9?

verseByVerse.quote: We want you to know, brothers, about the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia, for in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now, friends, we want to tell you about the grace God has given to the churches of Macedonia. In a severe test of suffering, their overflowing joy and their deep poverty have overflowed into rich generosity.

The Macedonian churches. Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea (Acts 16–17). They were persecuted from the start (1 Thessalonians 1:6; 2:14; Philippians 1:29–30), and the region as a whole was poorer than wealthy Corinth.

The grace of God. Paul does not begin with what they gave but with what God gave them. Generosity is a work of grace. The word charis (grace) appears ten times in chapters 8–9, meaning God’s favour, the gift itself, and thanks.

A strange equation. Affliction + joy + extreme poverty = a wealth of generosity. Not wealth leading to generosity, but joy in God overflowing from poor people.

Extreme poverty. Literally “down-to-the-depths poverty”.

On a Tuesday. Some of the most generous Christians are the poorest. A church in Nigeria, Brazil or the Philippines sending missionaries and money to others puts many wealthy Western churches to shame. If you are waiting to be richer before you give, the Macedonians answer you.
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 8–9 concern the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. The Macedonian churches — Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea — were poor and persecuted.

verseByVerse.quote: For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord, begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints—
verseByVerse.commentary:
I can testify that they gave as much as they could, and even beyond what they could. Entirely of their own accord, they begged us earnestly for the privilege of taking part in this service to God’s people.

Beyond their means. Like the widow who gave two small coins: “she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on” (Mark 12:44).

Of their own accord. Paul did not pressure them; apparently he had not even asked, thinking them too poor.

Begging for the favour. They begged to give. They saw giving as a privilege (charis, grace) and a fellowship (koinōnia, partnership).

On a Tuesday. Next time a church offering comes round, or a charity appeal arrives, treat it as a privilege, not an imposition.

parallels.desc: the widow gave out of her poverty

verseByVerse.quote: and this, not as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they did more than we hoped: first they gave themselves to the Lord, and then, by God’s will, to us.

Themselves first. The secret of Macedonian generosity. Their gift of money was the overflow of a gift of themselves. “Present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1). Once you belong entirely to the Lord, your money is his too.

Then to us. They also gave themselves to Paul’s mission: people like Epaphroditus (Philippians 2:25), Sopater, Aristarchus and Secundus (Acts 20:4).

On a Tuesday. Before deciding what to give, settle who you belong to. If you have given yourself to the Lord, the question changes from “How much of mine should I give to God?” to “How much of God’s should I keep for myself?”

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, we urged Titus that as he had started, so he should complete among you this act of grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we have urged Titus that, since he made a start on this act of grace among you, he should bring it to completion.

Titus. He began the collection in Corinth on an earlier visit, probably when he carried the tearful letter. Now he will return to finish it.

This grace. Paul calls the gift itself “grace”. Giving is not a tax but a grace given and passed on.

On a Tuesday. Is there a pledge or promise of giving that you started and never finished? Finish it.

verseByVerse.quote: But as you excel in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in our love for you—see that you excel in this act of grace also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You excel in everything: in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all eagerness, and in the love we have kindled in you. Make sure you excel in this act of grace too.

The Corinthians’ gifts. They were proud of their spiritual gifts: faith, eloquence, knowledge (1 Corinthians 1:5–7). Paul affirms them, then adds one more to excel in: giving.

A textual note. Manuscripts differ between “our love for you” (ESV, with the earliest papyrus and Vaticanus) and “your love for us” (KJV, with Sinaiticus and others). “Our love for you” is the harder reading, since we would expect Paul to list their qualities, and is probably original: the love Paul has for them and has awakened in them.

On a Tuesday. A church with excellent preaching, music and Bible knowledge can be stingy. Which of the gifts on Paul’s list is weakest in you?

verseByVerse.quote: I say this not as a command, but to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am not saying this as a command. I want to test how genuine your love is by comparing it with the eagerness of others.

Not a command. Paul could command (as an apostle) but does not. Giving under compulsion is not grace (9:7). This is one reason the New Testament gives no fixed percentage.

Is the tithe binding on Christians? Some Christians teach that the Old Testament tithe (ten per cent) remains a minimum duty (Malachi 3:10). Others, including this commentary, hold that the tithe belonged to the Mosaic system that supported the Levites and temple, and that the New Testament replaces it with grace-giving: willing, regular, proportionate and generous (1 Corinthians 16:2). Verdict: the tithe is not binding as a law, but many Christians rightly find ten per cent a useful starting point. Grace should lead to more generosity, not less. The Macedonians gave beyond their means.

Genuine. Love that never costs anything may not be real love.

On a Tuesday. Look at your bank statement. What does it say about what you love?

verseByVerse.quote: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: though he was rich, for your sake he became poor, so that through his poverty you might become rich.

The ultimate motive. Paul does not use guilt or pressure. He points to Christ. Every Christian practice, even fundraising, is grounded in the gospel.

Rich. In his eternal glory with the Father (John 17:5; Philippians 2:6).

Became poor. The incarnation and the cross. He took the form of a slave (Philippians 2:7), was born in a borrowed stable, had “nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9:58), and died naked on a cross, buried in a borrowed tomb.

You might become rich. In what sense?

Prosperity teachers say Christ became poor so that believers could become materially wealthy.

Verdict: the riches are spiritual: forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, eternal life, an inheritance (Ephesians 1:3–14). Paul himself was often hungry and poor (6:10; 11:27). If Christ’s poverty was meant to make us materially rich, the Macedonians in “extreme poverty” would have been failures, yet Paul holds them up as models. The point is the opposite: because Christ gave up his riches for us, we give up ours for others.

For worship. Charles Wesley: “He left his Father’s throne above, so free, so infinite his grace; emptied himself of all but love, and bled for Adam’s helpless race.”

verseByVerse.quote: And in this matter I give my judgment: this benefits you, who a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. So now finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is my advice on the matter, and it is for your good. A year ago you were the first not only to do something but to want to do it. Now finish what you started, so that your eagerness to want it may be matched by your completing it, according to what you have.

A year ago. Corinth had started first, before Macedonia, but then stalled during the conflict with Paul.

Desire and doing. Good intentions are not enough. Finish what you started.

Out of what you have. Not beyond realistic means. Paul is not asking them to go into debt.

On a Tuesday. Many people intend to make a will that includes gifts to the Lord’s work, to start regular giving, or to support a missionary. Do it this week.

verseByVerse.quote: For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the willingness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what they do not have.

Proportion, not amount. God measures a gift by the heart and by what is left, not by its size. A pound from a child’s pocket money can be a greater gift than a thousand from a millionaire.

What it does not mean. Not that the rich can give a little and call it enough. Proportionate giving means the more you have, the more you give.

On a Tuesday. If you are on a tight budget, do not feel guilty that you cannot give much. Give willingly what you can. God accepts it.

verseByVerse.quote: For I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened, but that as a matter of fairness your abundance at the present time should supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be fairness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not mean that others should be relieved while you are burdened, but that it should be a matter of fairness. At present your abundance should meet their need, so that later their abundance may meet your need. Then there will be fairness.

Fairness. Isotēs: equality, balance. Not that everyone has exactly the same, but that no believer should go without necessities while others have plenty.

Mutual. Today Corinth has plenty and Jerusalem is in need. Tomorrow it may be the other way round. The body of Christ shares.

What it does not mean. Some have read this as Christian socialism, requiring compulsory redistribution of wealth by the state. Paul is speaking of voluntary giving between churches, not state policy. Even in Jerusalem’s early sharing (Acts 2:44–45) property remained private: “While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own?” (Acts 5:4). Christians may disagree about economic policy; this text calls the church to voluntary, generous sharing.

On a Tuesday. Is there a believer in your church struggling with rent, food or heating? Before thinking of government or charities, ask whether God has put your abundance where it is to meet their need.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written, “Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Scripture says, “The one who gathered much had nothing left over, and the one who gathered little did not go short.”

Exodus 16:18. The manna in the wilderness. Each family gathered an omer per person. Some gathered more, some less, but when measured, everyone had enough. If anyone hoarded it, it bred worms.

The lesson. God provides enough for all his people. Hoarding while others lack goes against his design. In the wilderness God did it by miracle; in the church, he does it through generosity.

On a Tuesday. What are you storing up that could become manna with worms in it (compare Matthew 6:19–20)? Saving for the future is wise (Proverbs 6:6–8), but hoarding beyond need while others go without is not.

parallels.desc: whoever gathered much had nothing left over

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — Titus and the Brothers; Transparency in Giving
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God for Titus’s eagerness to return to Corinth and introduces two companions: a brother well known among the churches for his gospel work and chosen by the churches to travel with the gift, and another brother proven in many tests. The arrangement is deliberate. Paul wants the handling of the money to be honourable not only before the Lord but in the eyes of people, so that no one can accuse him. He commends these representatives of the churches and asks the Corinthians to show them openly the love that Paul has boasted of.
verseByVerse.theology: The principle of handling ministry finances with transparent accountability applies directly to all Christian organisations. Paul, who could have simply trusted his own integrity, insists on multiple overseers and transparent processes — because the integrity of the ministry is at stake not only in God’s sight but in the sight of the watching world. Financial scandal in Christian ministry has consistently damaged the gospel’s credibility; Paul’s precaution (v. 20) is prophylactic wisdom.
verseByVerse.examples: A mission organisation implements a new policy requiring two-signature approval for all expenditures over a certain threshold, and annual independent financial audits reported to the whole organisation. Some staff feel this implies distrust. This passage gives the theological rationale: the precautions are not about distrust of individuals but about protecting the honour of the Lord and the integrity of the ministry in the sight of those who would use any irregularity to attack the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you. For he not only accepted our appeal, but being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God, who has put into Titus’s heart the same eager concern for you that I have. He not only welcomed our request, but he is so keen that he is coming to you on his own initiative.

God put it in his heart. Titus’s concern is God’s gift. Even good motives in our co-workers are reasons to thank God.

His own accord. Paul asked, but Titus wanted to go anyway. The best service is willing.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for the people who care about your church as much as you do. Tell them.

verseByVerse.quote: With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel. And not only that, but he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us as we carry out this act of grace that is being ministered by us, for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our good will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With him we are sending the brother whom all the churches praise for his work in the gospel. More than that, he was chosen by the churches to travel with us as we carry out this gracious work, which we are doing for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our goodwill.

Who was he? Paul does not name him. Origen, Jerome and others guessed Luke, and the Anglican collect for St Luke’s Day uses this verse. Others suggest Barnabas, Silas, Apollos, or one of the men listed in Acts 20:4. Verdict: we do not know. The Corinthians knew, and that was enough.

Appointed by the churches. Cheirotonētheis: elected, literally “chosen by a show of hands”. The contributing churches chose their own representative to accompany the money.

For the glory of the Lord. The collection honours Christ, by showing the unity of his body and the reality of his grace.

On a Tuesday. Not every faithful servant is named. Many of God’s best workers are known only as “the brother” or “the sister”. Be content with that.
verseByVerse.note: The famous brother is unnamed; some early writers guessed Luke.

verseByVerse.quote: We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are taking this precaution so that no one can criticise us over how we handle this generous gift. For we are concerned to do what is right not only in the Lord’s eyes but also in the eyes of people.

Above suspicion. Paul was carrying a large sum of money across the empire. His opponents already accused him of exploiting the Corinthians (12:16–18). So he made sure others, chosen by the churches, travelled with it.

Proverbs 3:4. Paul echoes the Greek version: providing what is good “in the sight of God and man”. Integrity before God is primary, but reputation before people matters too, for the gospel’s sake.

On a Tuesday. Church treasurers, charity trustees and business owners: never handle money alone. Two signatures, open accounts, independent checks. It protects you and the gospel. (See the study on Christians in business, on auditors.)

verseByVerse.quote: And with them we are sending our brother whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters, but who is now more earnest than ever because of his great confidence in you. As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for your benefit. And as for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are also sending with them our brother, whom we have often tested in many ways and found eager, and who is now even more eager because of his great confidence in you. As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker in serving you. As for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, an honour to Christ.

A third man. Again unnamed, again tested and proven.

Messengers. Literally apostoloi, “apostles”: people sent by the churches on a specific mission. Not apostles of Christ in the sense of the Twelve and Paul, who were eyewitnesses of the risen Lord with authority over the churches (1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:7–9). The word could be used broadly (Philippians 2:25). This matters for modern claims to apostolic office: the foundational apostles were unique (Ephesians 2:20).

The glory of Christ. Faithful, ordinary Christian workers bring glory to Christ.

On a Tuesday. If you have been sent by your church, as a missionary, a delegate or a volunteer, you carry Christ’s honour. Act accordingly.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “messengers” is literally “apostles” — men sent by the churches.

verseByVerse.quote: So give proof before the churches of your love and of our boasting about you to these men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So show these men, in front of the churches, the proof of your love and of the reasons for our pride in you.

Before the churches. The delegates represent other churches. How Corinth treats them and how it gives will be reported. The whole Christian network was watching.

Proof. Endeixis: demonstration. Love that is claimed must be shown.

On a Tuesday. Show hospitality to visiting missionaries and preachers. They report back, and your love becomes encouragement to churches far away.

For worship. Thank God that Jesus became poor for you. Then decide on one gift this week that would make that thanks visible.
