9.title: Sowing Generously: The Cheerful Giver
9.overview:
Paul continues on the collection for Jerusalem. He has boasted to the Macedonians that Corinth was ready a year ago, and their eagerness stirred the Macedonians to give. Now he is sending the brothers ahead so that the Corinthian gift is ready when he arrives with Macedonian companions, as a willing gift and not something extracted under pressure.

Then he gives the principles of Christian giving. A farmer who sows sparingly reaps sparingly. Each should give what he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. God is able to make every grace overflow, so that his people always have enough and plenty left for every good work; he supplies seed to the sower and will multiply it, enriching them so that they can be generous in every way. And the result goes far beyond meeting needs in Jerusalem: it overflows in thanksgiving to God, proves the Gentiles’ obedience to the gospel, and binds Jewish believers to them in prayer and love. The chapter ends with praise for the gift behind every gift: “Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Sowing and Reaping; the Cheerful Giver; the Inexpressible Gift
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul says he hardly needs to write about the collection, since he has boasted of Corinth’s readiness to the Macedonians and it has spurred them on. He is sending the brothers ahead so that the gift is ready when he arrives with Macedonian companions, and is a generous gift rather than something extracted. Then come the principles. Giving is like sowing: the harvest matches the sowing. Each should give what they have decided in their heart, willingly, for God loves a cheerful giver. God is able to supply everything needed and more, so that his people can be generous in every good work; he provides seed and will multiply it. The gift will meet needs in Jerusalem, but it will also overflow in thanks to God, prove the Corinthians’ faith, and draw the Jerusalem believers to pray for them. Paul ends by thanking God for his gift, too great for words.
verseByVerse.theology:
The sowing-reaping principle in v. 6 must be held in tension with the warning against prosperity theology, and the passage itself supplies the correction three times over. Paul is not promising that generous financial giving will result in financial wealth. The reaping he describes is named in v. 10 as “the harvest of your righteousness” — moral integrity and fruitfulness in God’s sight. The supply God gives in that same verse is “seed to the sower and bread for food” — resources to live on and resources to give again — and it is the seed, not the bread, that he undertakes to multiply. Verse 11 then adds that the enriching is “to be generous in every way.” The giver is not made wealthy; he is kept supplied so that generosity can continue. The decisive counter-example is in the previous chapter: the man held up as the supreme giver at 8:9 became poor.

Verse 9 quotes Psalm 112:9. The psalm is a portrait of the man who fears the LORD, and it places distributing freely and giving to the poor among his identifying marks, alongside steadiness and courage — generosity as a feature of godliness rather than an optional extra of temperament. The clause Paul is after is “his righteousness endures forever”: the money is gone and cannot be pointed to, and what it produced does not go anywhere.

“God loves a cheerful giver” (v. 7) comes from the Greek Old Testament at Proverbs 22:8, which carries a line the Hebrew text does not — a blessing on the cheerful and generous man. Paul’s citation focuses the divine pleasure on the disposition of the giver: the motivation and the manner of giving are as important to God as the amount.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation uses a pledge campaign with carefully designed giving targets and social dynamics (recognising top givers, publishing goals) that effectively apply social pressure to giving. Many give generously as a result. But the pastor wonders whether the giving is cheerful or compelled. This passage challenges not the amount raised but the mechanism: “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (v. 7). The goal is not merely generous giving but the formation of cheerful givers — people who give because they have been gripped by the inexpressible gift of God and cannot hold back.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints, for I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year. And your zeal has stirred up most of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is really no need for me to write to you about this service to God’s people. I know how eager you are, and I keep boasting about it to the Macedonians, telling them that Achaia has been ready since last year. And your enthusiasm has stirred most of them to act.

Superfluous. A tactful opening: “I hardly need to write this.” Then he writes a whole chapter. Paul knows the Corinthians respond better to encouragement than to pressure.

Achaia and Macedonia. The two Roman provinces of Greece: Achaia in the south, with Corinth, and Macedonia in the north, with Philippi and Thessalonica. There was rivalry between them.

Two directions. In 8:1–5 Paul used Macedonia to encourage Corinth. Here he has used Corinth to encourage Macedonia. Each church’s example stirs the other. That is healthy, provided the motive is love, not competition.

Is chapter 9 a separate letter? Some scholars think chapters 8 and 9 were originally two separate notes about the collection, since chapter 9 seems to introduce the subject again. Verdict: no manuscript separates them, and “superfluous to write” reads naturally as Paul turning from the delegates (8:16–24) back to the gift itself. Nothing in the meaning depends on it.

On a Tuesday. When another church or Christian outdoes you in generosity, let it stir you, not shame you. And when you give, remember that others may be watching and encouraged.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia was southern Greece, including Corinth; Macedonia was to the north.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, as I said you would be. Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated—to say nothing of you—for being so confident.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you in this matter does not turn out to be empty, and so that you will be ready, as I said you would be. Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we would be humiliated, to say nothing of you, for having been so confident.

Embarrassment. Paul had told the Macedonians that Corinth was ready. If the Macedonian delegates arrived and found no money collected, both Paul and the Corinthians would be shamed.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (KJV “in this same confident boasting”) add “of boasting” after “confidence”. The earliest have only “in this confidence”. The addition makes explicit what the context implies.

What it does not mean. Paul is not manipulating them by shame. He is honest about the stakes: their reputation, his, and the gospel’s. Integrity means doing what you said you would do.

On a Tuesday. If you have pledged a gift, a building fund contribution or regular support, keep your word without needing to be chased.

verseByVerse.quote: So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go to you ahead of me and arrange in advance the generous gift you promised. Then it will be ready as a true gift of blessing, not something squeezed out of you.

Arrange in advance. Practical wisdom. Collecting in advance avoids pressure when Paul arrives. Compare his instruction to set money aside each Sunday “so that there will be no collecting when I come” (1 Corinthians 16:2).

Willing gift and exaction. Literally “as a blessing (eulogia) and not as greed (pleonexia)”. A gift given gladly is a blessing to giver and receiver. A gift extracted by pressure is closer to robbery, and makes the receiver look greedy.

On a Tuesday. Plan your giving. Decide in advance, set it aside, give regularly. It keeps giving from being driven by emotional appeals or guilt.

verseByVerse.quote: The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously.

The farmer. A farmer who hoards his seed has nothing to plant; a farmer who sows a handful gets a small crop. The one who sows the whole field gets a full harvest. Giving is not losing; it is sowing.

Old Testament wisdom. “One gives freely, yet grows all the richer” (Proverbs 11:24). “Whoever brings blessing will be enriched” (Proverbs 11:25). Jesus: “give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:38). “Whatever one sows, that will he also reap” (Galatians 6:7).

Seed faith? Some prosperity teachers call this the law of “seed faith”: give money to a ministry and God must return it to you multiplied, as financial wealth. Verdict: the harvest Paul promises is not chiefly money but “the harvest of your righteousness” (v. 10), enough for every good work (v. 8), and thanksgiving to God (v. 12). God does provide for the generous, but so that they can keep giving, not so that they can become rich. A gift given in order to get is not generosity at all.

On a Tuesday. When you give and your bank balance goes down, think like a farmer: the seed is in the ground. Watch for the harvest God gives, which may be in other people’s lives more than in yours.

parallels.desc: one gives freely, yet grows all the richer

verseByVerse.quote: Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each of you should give what you have made up your mind to give, not reluctantly or because you feel forced, for God loves a cheerful giver.

Decided in the heart. Giving is personal and deliberate. Not set by an outside rule or a sudden impulse, but thought through before God.

Not reluctantly. Literally “not out of grief”: not with a pang of regret. Moses said the same: “You shall give to him freely, and your heart shall not be grudging when you give to him” (Deuteronomy 15:10).

Not under compulsion. Not because a leader pressured you or because everyone is watching. Another reason the New Testament gives no fixed tithe.

A cheerful giver. Paul echoes the Greek version of Proverbs 22:8, which adds that God blesses a cheerful man who gives. “Cheerful” is hilaros, from which we get “hilarious”: glad, joyful. God loves this, because it reflects himself, the God who gives gladly.

What it does not mean. Not that you should wait until you feel cheerful before giving. Give, and ask God for the cheer. Joy often comes in the giving.

On a Tuesday. Next time you give, notice how you feel. If it is grudging, ask why. Then remember what God has given you, and give again with thanks.

parallels.desc: from every man whose heart moves him
the Greek Old Testament adds a line about God blessing a cheerful giver

verseByVerse.quote: And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God is able to pour out every kind of grace on you in abundance, so that in every way and at every time you have all you need, and plenty left over for every good work.

God is able. The answer to the giver’s fear: “If I give, will I have enough?” God can provide.

All, every, always. The Greek piles them up: all grace, all sufficiency, in all things, at all times, every good work. Paul cannot say it strongly enough.

Sufficiency. Autarkeia, the word for contentment in Philippians 4:11: having enough. Not luxury, but enough, with enough over to give.

For good works. God supplies us so that we can give and serve (Ephesians 2:10). Provision is for overflow, not storage.

On a Tuesday. If fear is holding you back from giving, test this verse in a small way. Give a little more than feels safe, and watch how God provides.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Scripture says, “He has scattered his gifts freely and given to the poor; his righteousness lasts for ever.”

Psalm 112:9. Psalm 112 describes the man who fears the Lord: gracious, merciful, generous, lending freely. Paul quotes it word for word from the Greek version.

Who is “he”? Some take it as God, who scatters gifts. But in Psalm 112 “he” is the righteous man, and Psalm 111, its twin, says the same of God (111:3). Verdict: the generous believer, who reflects the generous God. His righteousness, his practical goodness, outlasts him.

Distributed freely. Eskorpisen: scattered, like a farmer sowing seed by hand. The picture of verse 6 again.

What it does not mean. Not that giving earns righteousness before God. “Righteousness” here means the righteous life that flows from faith, its good deeds remembered by God (Hebrews 6:10).

On a Tuesday. Long after your house is sold and your savings spent, the good you did for the poor will still be bearing fruit. Invest there.

parallels.desc: he has distributed freely; he has given to the poor

verseByVerse.quote: He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who provides seed for the sower and bread for food will also provide and multiply your seed for sowing, and will increase the harvest of your righteousness.

Isaiah 55:10. The rain and snow water the earth, “giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater.” God is the farmer’s provider. Without his rain and sun, no seed grows.

Seed and bread. Some of what God gives is for eating (our needs); some is seed (for giving). Wise stewards know the difference and do not eat their seed.

The harvest of your righteousness. Echoing Hosea 10:12: “Sow for yourselves righteousness; reap steadfast love.” The harvest is good deeds, changed lives and thanksgiving.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (KJV “minister bread for your food, and multiply your seed”) read the verbs as a wish (“may he supply”). The earliest read them as a promise (“he will supply”). The promise is original.

On a Tuesday. When you get a pay rise or an unexpected gift, ask: how much of this is bread, and how much is seed?

parallels.desc: seed to the sower and bread to the eater

verseByVerse.quote: You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way, which through us will produce thanksgiving to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will be made rich in every way so that you can be generous in every way, and your generosity, delivered through us, will produce thanksgiving to God.

Enriched to be generous. The purpose of God’s enrichment is generosity, not accumulation. You are a channel, not a reservoir.

In every way. Not only money: time, skills, hospitality, encouragement.

Thanksgiving. The final goal: God praised. The Jerusalem believers will thank God when the money arrives.

On a Tuesday. A retired teacher with time to spare can tutor a struggling child for free. A plumber can fix a widow’s boiler. Being enriched “in every way” means being generous “in every way”.

verseByVerse.quote: For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God. By their approval of this service, they will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ, and the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this service you are performing does not only supply the needs of God’s people; it also overflows in many thanks to God. Because this service proves who you are, people will praise God for your obedience to your confession of the gospel of Christ, and for the generosity of your sharing with them and with everyone.

Service. Leitourgia: from which we get “liturgy”. In Greek cities this was the public service a wealthy citizen performed at his own expense, such as funding a festival or a warship. In the Greek Old Testament it was priestly service in the temple. Giving is worship.

Proof. Dokimē: the tested genuineness of their faith. The Jewish believers in Jerusalem had doubts about Paul’s Gentile converts (Acts 21:20–21). A generous gift from them would prove the reality of their faith.

Submission to the confession. Their giving shows that their confession of the gospel is real and obeyed. Faith shows itself in works (James 2:18).

Unity. The collection bound Jewish and Gentile churches together. Paul risked his life to deliver it (Romans 15:30–31; Acts 21–24), and later told Felix, “I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings” (Acts 24:17).

And with all others. Christian generosity starts with the household of faith but does not stop there (Galatians 6:10).

On a Tuesday. Giving across divides, to a church of another culture, nation or tradition, is a powerful witness to the unity of Christ’s body. Consider supporting a persecuted church abroad.

verseByVerse.quote: while they long for you and pray for you, because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in their prayers for you they will long for you, because of the extraordinary grace God has given you.

Prayer in return. The Jerusalem believers had little money to give, but they could pray. Material gifts flow one way; prayer and love flow back.

Long for you. People who had never met would feel affection for each other through giving and prayer. That is the body of Christ.

Surpassing grace. Again, the gift is God’s grace in the Corinthians.

On a Tuesday. When you receive help from someone, pray for them by name. It is what you can give back.

verseByVerse.quote: Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thanks be to God for his gift, which is too great for words!

The gift. After two chapters about the Corinthians’ gift, Paul ends with God’s. Most interpreters take it as Christ himself, the gift behind every gift: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son” (John 3:16). Some take it as the grace that unites Jews and Gentiles, shown in the collection. Verdict: ultimately Christ; the grace of 8:9 frames both chapters.

Inexpressible. Anekdiēgētos: indescribable, impossible to tell in full. Perhaps Paul coined the word.

Why this motivates giving. “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). The God who gave the greatest gift will not leave generous givers short.

For worship. Stop and say Paul’s words aloud. Then sing: “Thank you, O my Father, for giving us your Son.”

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints,<sup>2</sup>for I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year. And your zeal has stirred up most of them.<sup>3</sup>But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, as I said you would be.<sup>4</sup>Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated—to say nothing of you—for being so confident.<sup>5</sup>So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction.<sup>6</sup>The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.<sup>7</sup>Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.<sup>8</sup>And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.<sup>9</sup>As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”<sup>10</sup>He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.<sup>11</sup>You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way, which through us will produce thanksgiving to God.<sup>12</sup>For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God.<sup>13</sup>By their approval of this service, they will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ, and the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others,<sup>14</sup>while they long for you and pray for you, because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.<sup>15</sup>Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!

10.title: Divine Weapons and Boasting in the Lord
10.overview:
With chapter 10 the tone changes sharply. Chapters 1–9 are warm and relieved; chapters 10–13 are a fierce defence against the visiting teachers Paul will call “super-apostles” and “false apostles”. Some scholars therefore think these chapters were a separate letter, either the earlier tearful letter (2:4) or a later one written after fresh bad news. No manuscript divides the letter, and Paul may simply turn here from the repentant majority to the minority still under the rivals’ influence. Either way, these chapters are Scripture and their meaning is clear.

The rivals mocked Paul: bold in letters but feeble in person, a poor speaker, an unimpressive man. Paul answers that he appeals by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, but he is not powerless. His weapons are not worldly ones (rhetoric, manipulation, status), but divine power that demolishes strongholds of false reasoning and takes every thought captive to obey Christ. What he writes when absent he will do when present. He refuses to measure himself against others who commend themselves. He keeps to the field God assigned him, which reached as far as Corinth, and hopes to go beyond it. The only boast that counts is in the Lord, and the only commendation that counts is the Lord’s.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Weapons of Divine Warfare
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tone sharpens as Paul answers rivals who mock him as timid in person and bold only on paper. He appeals to them with the gentleness of Christ, hoping he will not have to act firmly against those who accuse him of worldly motives. He does live as a weak human being, but he does not fight with worldly methods. His weapons have God’s power to demolish fortresses of the mind: arguments and proud ideas raised against the knowledge of God. He aims to bring every thought under Christ’s rule, and is prepared to discipline persistent disobedience once the church as a whole is obedient.
verseByVerse.theology: The “weapons of warfare” in v. 4 are the weapons of gospel ministry: the proclaimed word, prayer, the demonstration of transformed lives, the power of the Spirit. These are not powerful by worldly standards (rhetorical brilliance, social influence, political power) but divinely powerful for pulling down strongholds. This is the consistent NT theology of ministry: God chooses the weak and foolish things to shame the strong and wise (1 Cor. 1:27), precisely so that the power is unmistakably his. The church that abandons the means God has ordained in favour of worldly methods of influence has swapped divinely powerful weapons for humanly impressive ones.
verseByVerse.examples: A church in a university town hires a communications consultant to help them “win the argument” with the secular culture. The consultant advises them to lead with culturally acceptable values rather than with gospel claims. This passage challenges the strategy: taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ is the goal, but the weapons for achieving it are not strategic communication management — they are the divinely powerful weapons of the gospel, prayer, and the demonstration of transformed lives. The strongholds that prevent the knowledge of God are spiritual, and only spiritual weapons can pull them down.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, myself entreat you, by the meekness and gentleness of Christ—I who am humble when face to face with you, but bold toward you when I am away!— I beg of you that when I am present I may not have to show boldness with such confidence as I count on showing against some who suspect us of walking according to the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I, Paul, appeal to you personally by the humility and gentleness of Christ. I am the one who, they say, is meek when face to face with you but bold when away! I beg you not to make me be bold when I come, with the confidence I expect to use against some who think we live by worldly standards.

I, Paul, myself. Emphatic. No Timothy as co-author now. This is personal.

Meekness and gentleness of Christ. Prautēs (meekness, strength under control) and epieikeia (gentleness, forbearance, not insisting on one’s rights; see Philippians 4:5). Jesus said, “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). Paul’s critics thought his gentleness was weakness. Paul says it is the manner of Christ himself.

Humble face to face. Paul quotes their sneer. In Greek culture, tapeinos (humble, lowly) was an insult: servile, cringing. Paul had come to Corinth “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3).

Walking according to the flesh. They accused him of worldly motives: weakness, fickleness, self-interest.

On a Tuesday. Gentleness is not weakness. A father who does not shout, a manager who does not bully, can still be firm. Meekness is strength under Christ’s control.
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 10–13 answer rival teachers at Corinth who belittled Paul.

parallels.desc: Moses was very meek

verseByVerse.quote: For though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For although we live as human beings, we do not fight our battles in a merely human way. The weapons we use are not the world’s weapons. They have God’s power to tear down fortresses.

In the flesh, not according to the flesh. Paul is human and weak, but his methods are not worldly. The distinction runs through the chapter.

Weapons. The world’s weapons in Corinth were rhetoric, flattery, social status, money and intimidation. Paul’s weapons are the truth of the gospel, prayer, the word of God and the Spirit (6:7; Ephesians 6:10–18).

Strongholds. Ochyrōmata: fortresses, the strong towers of a besieged city. Corinth itself was overlooked by the Acrocorinth, a massive fortified hill. Proverbs 21:22 in the Greek version uses the same word: “A wise man scales the city of the mighty and brings down the stronghold in which they trust.”

What are the strongholds? Some Christians in the deliverance and “spiritual warfare” movements read them as territorial demons or spiritual powers over cities, to be bound by prayer. Verdict: Paul tells us what they are in the next verse: “arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God”. They are fortresses of the mind: false ideas, pride, ideologies. Satan works through them (4:4; Ephesians 6:12), and prayer matters, but the battle is won by truth.

On a Tuesday. When you face opposition at work or in an online debate, refuse the world’s weapons: sarcasm, manipulation, half-truths. Use truth, patience and prayer.
verseByVerse.note: Strongholds were fortified towers or citadels.

verseByVerse.quote: We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We tear down arguments and every proud barrier raised against the knowledge of God, and we take every thought prisoner to make it obey Christ.

Arguments. Logismoi: reasonings, ideas, worldviews. Paul engaged Greek philosophy (Acts 17:16–34) and Jewish argument. He did not avoid thinking; he demolished bad thinking.

Every lofty opinion. Hypsōma: a high thing, like a tower. Pride raised up against God, like the tower of Babel (Genesis 11:4).

Every thought captive. Military language: prisoners led away after a city falls. Every idea, in every field, is to be brought under Christ’s authority. Abraham Kuyper said there is not one square inch of all creation over which Christ does not cry “Mine!”

Apologetics. Christians defend the faith in different ways. Evidentialists begin with evidence common to everyone, such as history and the resurrection; presuppositionalists (Cornelius Van Til) argue that only the Christian worldview makes reason and evidence intelligible, and challenge the unbeliever’s assumptions. Verdict: both have a place. This verse supports the presuppositional insight that no thought is neutral; but Paul also used evidence (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Always “prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you” (1 Peter 3:15), with gentleness.

On a Tuesday. What you watch, read and listen to shapes your thoughts. Take some of it captive this week: ask of a news story or a film, “What does this assume about God and people? Is it true?”

verseByVerse.quote: being ready to punish every disobedience, when your obedience is complete.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And once your obedience is complete, we are ready to punish every act of disobedience.

Punish. Ekdikēsai: to bring justice, to discipline. Paul means church discipline, not civil punishment (13:2, 10).

When your obedience is complete. Paul waits until the church as a whole is with him, so that discipline is the church’s act, not a lone apostle’s. Then he will deal with the few who remain rebellious.

What it does not mean. Not that the church should use force, fines or state power against dissenters. Sadly, Christians have done so, with persecution of heretics and religious wars. The church’s weapons are spiritual (v. 4): admonition, exclusion from fellowship, and prayer for repentance.

On a Tuesday. If you are a church leader, deal with problems patiently, building consensus first. But do deal with them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul urges them to look at the facts. He belongs to Christ as much as anyone, and his authority was given to build them up, not tear them down. Some say his letters are impressive but he is feeble in person and a poor speaker; they will find him the same in action as on paper. He will not join those who rate themselves by comparing themselves with each other. His boasting stays within the field God assigned him, which included Corinth, where he was first to bring the gospel. He does not claim credit for others’ work, and hopes their growth will free him to preach further afield. In the end only one boast counts, boasting in the Lord, and only one approval, the Lord’s.
verseByVerse.theology: The criterion of the Lord’s commendation (v. 18) is the basis of all genuine ministerial authority in the NT. The super-apostles derive their authority from letters of recommendation (3:1), impressive personal presence, rhetorical skill, and visions and revelations (12:1). Paul derives his from the divine call (Gal. 1:1), the fruit of his ministry (the transformed Corinthians — 3:2), and ultimately from the Lord’s own assessment. This does not make Paul self-certifying; it means his legitimacy is determined at the bar of heaven, not at the bar of human opinion.
verseByVerse.examples: A minister with a large platform cultivates an online presence that constantly showcases his ministry’s results — attendance figures, conversion stories, speaking engagements, endorsements from well-known figures. He tells himself he is building credibility for the gospel. This passage asks a harder question: is he building the gospel’s credibility or his own? The test is not whether he mentions God in his self-promotion but whether his confidence is ultimately in the Lord’s assessment or in the metrics of human comparison.

verseByVerse.quote: Look at what is before your eyes. If anyone is confident that he is Christ’s, let him remind himself that just as he is Christ’s, so also are we. For even if I boast a little too much of our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you, I will not be ashamed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look at what is in front of you. If anyone is sure that they belong to Christ, they should think again: we belong to Christ just as much as they do. Even if I boast rather a lot about the authority the Lord gave us, I will not be ashamed of it, for he gave it to build you up, not to tear you down.

What is before your eyes. Either “look at the facts” (a command) or “you look only on the surface” (a statement). Both fit: the Corinthians judged by appearances, and the facts, their own conversion, prove Paul’s apostleship.

Christ’s. The rivals perhaps claimed a special connection with Christ, such as having known Jesus, or belonging to the Jerusalem circle, or visions (compare 1 Corinthians 1:12, “I follow Christ”). Paul says: so am I.

For building up. Authority in the church exists for the good of others (13:10). Any authority used to tear people down has been abused.

On a Tuesday. If you have authority, as a parent, an elder or a boss, ask whether the people under you are being built up or torn down by how you use it.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not want to appear to be frightening you with my letters. For they say, “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not want to seem to be trying to frighten you with my letters. For some say, “His letters are weighty and powerful, but in person he is weak, and his speaking is worthless.”

The insult. In the Greek world a teacher was judged by his presence and his speaking. Professional orators (sophists) trained voice, gesture and appearance and charged high fees. Paul did not use their techniques (1 Corinthians 2:1–4), so he looked amateur.

What did Paul look like? We do not know. A second-century romance, the Acts of Paul and Thecla, describes him as short, bald, bow-legged, with eyebrows meeting and a slightly hooked nose, yet full of grace. It may preserve a memory, or just legend. Paul may also have had a visible illness or disability (Galatians 4:13–14; 2 Corinthians 12:7).

What it does not mean. Not that good speaking is wrong. Apollos was eloquent (Acts 18:24) and Paul did not criticise him. But God does not judge by appearance: “man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

On a Tuesday. Do you judge preachers, leaders or new colleagues by how they look and sound? Ask instead whether they are faithful.
verseByVerse.note: Greek culture prized impressive physical presence and polished oratory.

verseByVerse.quote: Let such a person understand that what we say by letter when absent, we do when present.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People who say this should understand that what we say in our letters while absent, we will also do in person when we are present.

Consistency. Paul is not two people. The charge of fickleness from 1:17 again. What he writes, he will do.

On a Tuesday. Are you the same person online as in person, at home as at church? Integrity means one person everywhere.

verseByVerse.quote: Not that we dare to classify or compare ourselves with some of those who are commending themselves. But when they measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another, they are without understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We would not dare to class ourselves with, or compare ourselves to, some of those who recommend themselves. When they measure themselves by each other and compare themselves with each other, they show they have no understanding.

Irony. “We would not dare”: Paul is being ironic. He would not stoop to it.

Self-measurement. The rivals set their own standards and measured themselves against each other: a closed circle of mutual admiration. Like a group of short men deciding they are tall because they only stand beside each other.

A textual note. Some Western manuscripts omit the words “they are without understanding. But we”, so that the sentence describes Paul measuring himself by himself. The longer reading is far better attested and makes sense of the contrast; it is original.

On a Tuesday. Churches and Christians can compare themselves with others who are worse and feel good about it. Measure yourself by Christ, and by God’s word, not by other people.

verseByVerse.quote: But we will not boast beyond limits, but will boast only with regard to the area of influence God assigned to us, to reach even to you. For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach you. For we were the first to come all the way to you with the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we will not boast beyond proper limits. We will boast only within the field of work God has assigned us, a field that reaches even as far as you. We are not overreaching, as if we had never reached you; we were the first to come all the way to you with the gospel of Christ.

Area of influence. Kanōn: a measuring rod, then a measured area, an assigned field. (Later, the word was used for the “canon” of Scripture, the books measured as authoritative.) At the Jerusalem meeting, Paul’s field was agreed as the Gentiles (Galatians 2:7–9).

We were first. Paul founded the church in Corinth (Acts 18:1–11; 1 Corinthians 3:6, 10). The rivals came later and claimed his work.

On a Tuesday. Know your field. God gives each person a sphere: a family, a job, a church role, a neighbourhood. Be faithful there rather than envying another’s.

verseByVerse.quote: We do not boast beyond limit in the labors of others. But our hope is that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you may be greatly enlarged, so that we may preach the gospel in lands beyond you, without boasting of work already done in another’s area of influence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We do not boast beyond limits about work others have done. Our hope is that as your faith grows, our field of work among you will be greatly enlarged, so that we can preach the gospel in the regions beyond you, without boasting about work already done in someone else’s field.

The labours of others. The rivals were taking credit for Paul’s work. Paul’s principle was the opposite: “I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else’s foundation” (Romans 15:20).

Lands beyond. West of Corinth lay Italy and Spain. Paul planned to go to Rome and then Spain (Romans 15:24, 28). The Corinthians’ growth would free him to go further.

On a Tuesday. A mature church releases people and money for mission elsewhere. Is your church only growing, or also sending?
verseByVerse.note: Paul hoped to go on to Rome and Spain.

verseByVerse.quote: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.” For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.” For it is not the person who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.

Jeremiah 9:23–24. “Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me.” Paul quoted the same summary in 1 Corinthians 1:31. Wisdom, power and wealth were exactly what Corinth boasted in.

The Lord’s commendation. Self-promotion counts for nothing. What counts is the Lord’s verdict on the last day: “Then each one will receive his commendation from God” (1 Corinthians 4:5). “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21).

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to drop a hint about your achievements, at a dinner party, on LinkedIn or in a church meeting, boast instead in the Lord, or say nothing.

For worship. Thank God for one thing he has done through you, and give him the credit for it.

parallels.desc: let him who boasts boast in this

11.title: The Fool's Speech and the Catalogue of Suffering
11.overview:
In this chapter Paul does something he finds distasteful: he boasts. The rival teachers in Corinth commended themselves loudly, with their Jewish pedigree, eloquence, visions and fees, and the Corinthians were impressed. So Paul plays “the fool” for a while, borrowing their method to expose it. He fears the church is being seduced away from Christ, like Eve by the serpent, by teachers who bring a different Jesus, a different spirit and a different gospel. He defends his practice of preaching free of charge, which they took as a sign of inferiority, and unmasks the rivals as false apostles, servants of Satan disguised as servants of righteousness.

Then comes the “fool’s speech” proper. Paul matches their credentials, Hebrew, Israelite, descendant of Abraham, and then lists not his successes but his sufferings: floggings, beatings, a stoning, shipwrecks, dangers on every road, hunger, cold and the daily weight of care for all the churches. The climax is deliberately absurd: his greatest exploit was being lowered in a basket through a window to escape from Damascus. If he must boast, he will boast of his weakness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Jealousy for the Corinthians and the False Apostles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks the Corinthians to put up with a little foolishness from him, because he loves them with God’s own jealousy: he promised them to Christ like a bride to her husband, and fears they are being led away from simple, pure devotion to Christ, as Eve was deceived by the serpent. They tolerate teachers who preach another Jesus and another gospel, yet Paul is in no way inferior to these so-called super-apostles, even if he is no polished speaker. Was it wrong of him to preach to them free of charge, taking support from other churches instead? He will keep refusing their money, to cut the ground from under those who want to claim equal status with him. These men are false apostles disguised as apostles of Christ, which is no surprise, since Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light; they will end as their deeds deserve.
verseByVerse.theology: The identification of false apostles as servants of Satan (v. 15) is one of Paul’s most severe theological statements. It raises the question of how to identify false apostles — since they come disguised as servants of righteousness. The test that Paul has been applying throughout the letter is: what is the content of the message? What is the character of the minister? Does the ministry bear the cruciform pattern of genuine apostolic suffering? Paul’s opponents fail all three tests: their message is a different gospel; their character is self-promotional; their lives show no evidence of the suffering that authentic ministry requires.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation is attracted to a visiting teacher who is eloquent, radiantly confident, and preaches a message of spiritual empowerment, prosperity, and supernatural experience — all framed in Christian language. The pastor is concerned but cannot point to an obviously heretical statement. This passage gives him the categories: the test is not merely whether Jesus is mentioned but which Jesus is being presented, which spirit is being invoked, which gospel is being preached. The angel-of-light disguise means the most dangerous false teaching often looks impressively spiritual.

verseByVerse.quote: I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Do bear with me! For I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hope you will put up with a little foolishness from me; please do. I am jealous for you with the jealousy of God himself, because I promised you in marriage to one husband, Christ, and I want to present you to him as a pure bride.

Foolishness. Paul is about to boast, which he regards as foolish (v. 17). He apologises in advance.

Divine jealousy. Not envy, but the protective zeal of a husband for his wife. God calls himself jealous in this sense (Exodus 34:14) and pictures his people as his bride (Hosea 2:19–20).

The betrothal. In Jewish custom, betrothal was a binding commitment, a year or so before the wedding. The bride’s father guarded her purity until he handed her to the groom. Paul, as the Corinthians’ spiritual father (1 Corinthians 4:15), arranged the betrothal when he preached Christ to them, and must present them pure on the wedding day, Christ’s return (Ephesians 5:27; Revelation 19:7).

On a Tuesday. The Christian life is a betrothal. Faithfulness to Christ is not a rule but a love story. When you drift towards other loves, remember whose you are.
verseByVerse.note: In a Jewish betrothal the bride was already bound to her husband-to-be, and her purity was guarded until the wedding; Paul pictures himself in that guardian role.

parallels.desc: I will betroth you to me forever

verseByVerse.quote: But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I am afraid that, just as the serpent tricked Eve with his cunning, your minds may be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.

The serpent. Genesis 3. Satan did not attack Eve with force but with clever words that twisted God’s word: “Did God actually say?” (Genesis 3:1). False teachers work the same way.

Your thoughts. The battlefield is the mind (10:5).

Sincere and pure devotion. Haplotēs, simplicity: single-minded, undivided loyalty. Not intellectual simplicity, but a heart wholly given to Christ.

A textual note. The earliest manuscripts read “sincere and pure devotion”. Later ones (followed by the KJV, “the simplicity that is in Christ”) lack “and pure”. The longer reading is probably original.

On a Tuesday. Satan rarely tells you to abandon Christ. He suggests Christ plus something: Christ plus a technique, a political cause, an experience. Keep your devotion simple.

parallels.desc: the serpent deceived me

verseByVerse.quote: For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus than the one we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit from the one you received, or if you accept a different gospel from the one you accepted, you put up with it readily enough.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if someone comes and preaches a different Jesus from the one we preached, or you receive a different spirit from the one you received, or a different gospel from the one you accepted, you put up with it easily enough.

A different Jesus. The name was the same, but the content was different. Perhaps a Jesus of power and success without the cross, or a Jesus who required law-keeping. Every heresy has its own Jesus.

A different spirit. Not the Holy Spirit, who brings freedom (3:17), but a spirit of bondage, pride or fear (Romans 8:15).

A different gospel. Compare Galatians 1:6–9: there is no other gospel.

Who were the rivals? Scholars disagree.

Judaizers, like those in Galatia, insisting on the law (they are Hebrews, v. 22).

Hellenistic Jewish preachers who presented themselves as “divine men”, impressive speakers with miracles and visions.

In the nineteenth century F. C. Baur argued they represented the Jerusalem apostles themselves, in conflict with Paul.

Verdict: Jewish Christian missionaries who boasted of their Jewish credentials and their spiritual power, perhaps claiming the backing of Jerusalem. But they were not the Twelve: Paul speaks of the Jerusalem apostles with respect elsewhere (Galatians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 15:5–11), and the “super-apostles” are the same men he calls false apostles (v. 13).

On a Tuesday. When you hear a preacher, test not only whether he mentions Jesus, but which Jesus. Is he the crucified and risen Lord of the Bible?

verseByVerse.quote: Indeed, I consider that I am not in the least inferior to these super-apostles. Even if I am unskilled in speaking, I am not so in knowledge; indeed, in every way we have made this plain to you in all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not think I am in the least inferior to these “super-apostles”. I may be untrained as a speaker, but I am not lacking in knowledge; we have made that perfectly clear to you in every way.

Super-apostles. Hyperlian apostoloi: “extra-super apostles”. Paul’s sarcastic name for the rivals.

Unskilled in speaking. Idiōtēs: an amateur, a layman, without professional rhetorical training. Paul admits he does not perform like a sophist. But his letters show he could write powerfully (10:10), and his speeches in Acts are effective.

Not in knowledge. He knows the truth: the gospel, revealed by Christ (Galatians 1:12).

On a Tuesday. Do not dismiss a preacher because he is not polished, or follow one because he is. Ask what he knows of God and whether it is true.
verseByVerse.note: “Super-apostles” is Paul’s ironic name for the rival teachers.

verseByVerse.quote: Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached God’s gospel to you free of charge? I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or did I do something wrong by humbling myself so that you could be lifted up, preaching God’s gospel to you without charge? I took support from other churches, robbing them, so to speak, in order to serve you.

The patronage system. In Corinth, as across the Roman world, teachers and philosophers were usually supported by wealthy patrons, and a teacher who accepted support became the patron’s client, under obligation. Teachers also charged fees, and a high fee signalled high status. Paul refused both, working with his hands as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3). The Corinthians apparently took this as a sign that he was second-rate, or that he did not love them, or that he was too proud to accept their gifts.

Why did Paul refuse? So that no one could say he preached for money (1 Corinthians 9:12, 15–18), so that he would not be anyone’s client, and to follow Christ who made himself poor (8:9).

Robbed. A strong word, used of plundering a defeated enemy. Hyperbole: he accepted money from poorer churches (Macedonia) to serve the richer Corinthians for free.

What it does not mean. Not that ministers should never be paid. Paul defends the right of ministers to support (1 Corinthians 9:4–14; Galatians 6:6). He chose to waive it in Corinth for the gospel’s sake.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes the most loving thing is to refuse a gift that would come with strings attached.

verseByVerse.quote: And when I was with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. So I refrained and will refrain from burdening you in any way. As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I was with you and needed something, I did not become a burden to anyone, because the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I needed. I kept myself from being a burden to you in any way, and I will go on doing so. As surely as Christ’s truth is in me, no one in all Achaia will stop me boasting about this.

From Macedonia. Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia with support from the Philippians, and then Paul was able to devote himself fully to preaching (Acts 18:5; Philippians 4:15).

Not a burden. Katanarkaō: originally to grow numb, then to be a dead weight on someone.

This boasting. Paul’s one boast: that he preached for free.

On a Tuesday. If you serve in church, aim to give more than you take.

verseByVerse.quote: And why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do! And what I am doing I will continue to do, in order to undermine the claim of those who would like to claim that in their boasted mission they work on the same terms as we do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do! And I will go on doing what I am doing, to cut the ground from under those who would like to be seen as working on the same terms as we do in the things they boast about.

Do I not love you? The rivals may have said Paul’s refusal showed he did not love them. Paul answers with an oath: God knows.

Undermine the claim. The rivals took money and would like to say they were just like Paul. As long as Paul refuses payment, they cannot make that claim.

On a Tuesday. Love is sometimes misread. Keep loving anyway, and let God be your witness.

verseByVerse.quote: For such men are false apostles, deceitful workmen, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Such people are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. That is not surprising, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.

False apostles. Pseudapostoloi: perhaps a word Paul coined. They claim to be sent by Christ but are not.

Deceitful workers. They look like gospel workers; they are frauds.

Angel of light. Scripture does not record Satan appearing this way, but Jewish tradition did. In one text (the Life of Adam and Eve) Satan takes the form of an angel of brightness to deceive Eve a second time. The point: evil rarely looks evil. It looks bright, attractive, spiritual.

Testing. Jesus warned of false prophets “in sheep’s clothing” (Matthew 7:15). John: “test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1). The test is the gospel (v. 4) and the fruit (Matthew 7:16).

On a Tuesday. A charismatic, popular, attractive teacher may be false. Do not judge by brightness. Judge by the message and the life.

verseByVerse.quote: So it is no surprise if his servants, also, disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So it is no great thing if his servants also disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. They will come to the end their actions deserve.

Servants of righteousness. Perhaps they spoke much about righteousness, law and moral reform. They seemed upright.

Their end. Judgement according to deeds (5:10; Romans 2:6). Paul leaves them to God.

On a Tuesday. You do not need to expose every false teacher yourself. Warn others where needed, and trust God to judge.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–33 — The Fool’s Boast and the Catalogue of Sufferings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul says again that he is not really a fool, but if they insist on thinking so, they can let him boast a little like one. He admits that this kind of boasting is not how the Lord would speak; it is the way of the flesh, which the rivals practise. The Corinthians, so wise in their own eyes, happily put up with fools, and even with leaders who enslave, exploit, take advantage, act superior and slap them in the face. Paul confesses, ironically, that he was too weak for that. Then he matches the rivals’ claims: like them he is a Hebrew, an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, and as a servant of Christ he outdoes them, in labours, imprisonments, beatings and near-deaths. He lists floggings in the synagogues, Roman beatings, a stoning, three shipwrecks and a night and day adrift, and every kind of danger on his travels, along with toil, sleeplessness, hunger, thirst, cold and exposure. On top of all that comes the daily pressure of concern for all the churches; he feels every believer’s weakness and burns over every one who is made to stumble. If he must boast, he will boast of his weakness, and he swears before God that he is telling the truth. He ends with an anti-climax: at Damascus, when the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city to arrest him, he escaped by being let down through a window in a basket.
verseByVerse.theology: The catalogue of sufferings is Paul’s primary credential. In his opponents’ world, apostolic legitimacy was demonstrated by impressive spiritual experiences (visions, tongues, miraculous signs) and social credibility (letters of recommendation, personal charisma, philosophical sophistication). Paul’s credential is precisely the opposite: a body broken by service, a life spent in the pattern of the cross. This is not masochism; it is the coherence of messenger and message. The one who preaches a crucified Christ must bear in his body the pattern of the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: A church’s senior pastor has served for 25 years in a difficult context: modest attendance, a neighbourhood in decline, countless crises with little visible breakthrough. When a search committee from a larger church comes to interview him, they ask about his “greatest ministry successes.” He does not know what to say. This passage suggests a different category: the 25-year record of faithfulness in hardship, the daily anxiety for the congregation, the pattern of showing up — this is the apostolic credential. The question “what have you built?” is not the only or even the primary question.

verseByVerse.quote: I repeat, let no one think me foolish. But even if you do, accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. What I am saying with this boastful confidence, I say not as the Lord would but as a fool. Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I say again: no one should think I am a fool. But if you do, then accept me as a fool, so that I too can do a little boasting. What I am saying in this boastful confidence is not the way the Lord would speak; I am speaking as a fool. Since many boast in worldly terms, I will boast too.

The fool’s speech. In Greek drama and rhetoric, the fool was a stock character who could say things others could not. Paul adopts the role ironically: he will imitate the rivals’ boasting to show how foolish it is.

Not as the Lord would. Paul is honest that this is not Christlike speech. Jesus did not boast. Paul does it only to win back the Corinthians.

What it does not mean. Not that these chapters are less inspired. Paul is deliberately using irony; the Spirit inspired the irony.

On a Tuesday. Irony and humour can be tools of truth. But use them, as Paul does, for love and not to wound.
verseByVerse.note: Paul adopts the rivals’ style of boasting to expose it, calling it foolishness.

verseByVerse.quote: For you gladly bear with fools, being wise yourselves! For you bear it if someone makes slaves of you, or devours you, or takes advantage of you, or puts on airs, or strikes you in the face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are so wise that you gladly put up with fools! You put up with anyone who enslaves you, who eats you up, who takes advantage of you, who puts on airs, or who slaps you in the face.

Biting irony. The Corinthians thought themselves wise (1 Corinthians 4:10). Yet they tolerated abusive leaders.

Five abuses. Enslaving (controlling them), devouring (living off their money), taking advantage, exalting themselves, and slapping them in the face (perhaps literally, or as public humiliation). Spiritual abuse is not new.

Why do people tolerate abusive leaders? Often because confidence and domination look like power and spirituality. A gentle leader can seem weak by comparison.

On a Tuesday. If your church leader controls, exploits, humiliates or bullies people, that is not strong leadership. It is the opposite of Christ’s. Speak to other leaders or seek help outside.

verseByVerse.quote: To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am ashamed to admit that we were too weak to do that!

Too weak. Supreme irony. Paul was “too weak” to abuse them. He accepts the charge of weakness and turns it into praise: weakness in that sense is Christlike.

On a Tuesday. If you are criticised for being too gentle as a parent, a manager or a pastor, check whether you are failing to lead. But if the complaint is that you will not bully, take it as a compliment.

verseByVerse.quote: Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they Abraham’s descendants? So am I.

Three credentials. Hebrews: ethnically Jewish, perhaps speaking Hebrew or Aramaic (Philippians 3:5). Israelites: members of God’s covenant people. Offspring of Abraham: heirs of the promise. The rivals were apparently proud of their Jewish pedigree.

So am I. Paul matches them point for point. But he has already said what this is worth compared with Christ (Philippians 3:7–8).

On a Tuesday. Christian background, family history or denominational pedigree counts for nothing before God. Christ is everything.

verseByVerse.quote: Are they servants of Christ? I am a better one—I am talking like a madman—with far greater labors, far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, and often near death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are they servants of Christ? I am more so, and I am talking like a madman. I have worked much harder, been in prison far more often, been flogged more times than I can count, and faced death again and again.

I am a better one. Paul catches himself: “I am talking like a madman”. Even playing the fool, comparing oneself with other servants of Christ feels insane.

The proof. Not converts, churches, miracles or visions, but sufferings. A servant of Christ is known by how much he has suffered for Christ.

Imprisonments. Acts records only one before this letter (Philippi, Acts 16). Paul was clearly imprisoned more often than Acts tells.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to measure your Christian life by success, measure it by faithfulness under pressure instead.

verseByVerse.quote: Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five times the Jews gave me the thirty-nine lashes. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I was shipwrecked; I spent a night and a day adrift on the open sea.

Forty less one. The law allowed forty lashes and no more (Deuteronomy 25:3). To avoid miscounting, synagogue courts gave thirty-nine. The Mishnah describes it: thirteen strokes on the chest and twenty-six on the back, with a strap of calfskin, while the offender was bent over. Men sometimes died under it. Paul accepted this five times, which shows he kept going to synagogues and submitting to their discipline in order to preach to his own people.

Rods. A Roman punishment: the lictors who attended magistrates carried bundles of rods (the fasces). At Philippi Paul and Silas were beaten this way (Acts 16:22–23), illegally, since Paul was a Roman citizen (Acts 16:37; 22:25).

Stoned. At Lystra; he was dragged out of the city and left for dead (Acts 14:19).

Shipwrecked. Three times, all before the famous shipwreck of Acts 27, which came later. Sea travel was dangerous and Paul travelled constantly.

On a Tuesday. Most Christians in the West will never suffer like this. Many Christians in other parts of the world do. Pray for them by name, and support organisations that help persecuted believers.
verseByVerse.note: The law allowed up to forty lashes; the synagogues gave thirty-nine to be sure of not exceeding it. Beating with rods was a Roman punishment. The shipwrecks were before the one described in Acts 27.

parallels.desc: Paul stoned at Lystra
beaten with rods at Philippi

verseByVerse.quote: on frequent journeys, in danger from rivers, danger from robbers, danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles, danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea, danger from false brothers; in toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have been constantly on the move, in danger from rivers, from bandits, from my own people and from Gentiles, in danger in towns, in the wilderness and at sea, and in danger from false believers. I have worked hard and gone without sleep many times; I have been hungry and thirsty, often without food, cold and without enough clothing.

Eight dangers. Rivers in flood, with few bridges, in the mountains of Asia Minor. Robbers on lonely roads, such as the Taurus mountains between Perga and Pisidian Antioch, notorious for bandits. Jews who opposed him (Acts 9:23; 14:19; 17:5) and Gentiles (Acts 16; 19). Cities, deserts and seas. And “false brothers”: perhaps the worst danger, betrayal from inside the church (Galatians 2:4).

Toil and hardship. Working night and day at his trade so as not to burden anyone (1 Thessalonians 2:9).

Cold and exposure. Remember his request for his cloak from prison (2 Timothy 4:13).

On a Tuesday. Missionaries today still face danger, exhaustion and loneliness. Write to one this week and ask what they need.
verseByVerse.note: Rivers without bridges could be deadly in flood; roads through the mountains were infested with robbers.

verseByVerse.quote: And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And besides everything else, there is the pressure I feel every day: my concern for all the churches.

The heaviest burden. After the physical sufferings comes the inward one. “Pressure” (epistasis) is a crowd pressing in, or a constant weight. “Anxiety” (merimna) is the word Jesus used when he said not to be anxious (Matthew 6:25). Here it is right concern, the care of a pastor’s heart.

All the churches. Paul carried Corinth, Galatia, Philippi, Thessalonica, Ephesus and many others in his heart.

On a Tuesday. Your pastor carries this weight too. Pray for him, encourage him, and do not add to the pressure needlessly.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant? If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is weak, and I do not feel weak too? Who is made to stumble into sin, and I do not burn with anger? If I have to boast, I will boast about the things that show how weak I am.

Weak with the weak. Paul identifies with struggling believers (1 Corinthians 9:22). He does not stand above them.

Indignant. Literally “I burn”: with grief and anger when someone is led into sin. Jesus spoke strongly about those who cause little ones to stumble (Matthew 18:6).

Boast of weakness. The turning point of the speech, and the key to chapters 10–13. Paul’s glory is in his weakness, because there Christ’s power is seen (12:9–10).

On a Tuesday. Notice when a fellow believer is struggling. Do you feel it with them? Are you angry at what is harming them?

verseByVerse.quote: The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying. At Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize me, but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, who is to be praised for ever, knows I am not lying. In Damascus, the governor serving King Aretas had the city guarded so that he could arrest me. But I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped.

An oath. Paul solemnly swears that what follows is true, perhaps because it is so humiliating.

Aretas. Aretas IV, king of the Nabataean Arabs (capital Petra), who ruled about 9 BC to AD 40. His “ethnarch” was guarding Damascus, perhaps commanding the Nabataean community there or controlling the city for a period. Acts 9:23–25 says the Jews plotted to kill Paul and watched the gates; Paul’s disciples let him down through an opening in the wall in a basket. The two accounts complement each other: Paul had preached in Nabataean Arabia (Galatians 1:17), angering both groups.

The point. In the Roman army, the first soldier to climb over the wall of a besieged city received a special award, the “wall crown” (corona muralis). Paul’s greatest exploit? Going down a wall, in a basket, at night, running away. It is a deliberate anti-climax. He boasts of the most undignified moment of his career.

On a Tuesday. Can you tell your own story with your weakest moments in it? Christ is often most visible there.

For worship. Thank God that his power is shown in weak people, including you.
verseByVerse.note: Aretas IV was king of the Nabataeans, whose kingdom lay south and east of Damascus; he died around AD 40.
